timeline_entries.title: Puget Sound Becomes a Saltwater Body
timeline_entries.description: As the Vashon glacier retreats north of the Strait of Juan de Fuca, the freshwater proglacial lakes filling the Puget Sound basin reconnect with the Pacific Ocean, transforming the basin into a saltwater inland sea.
timeline_entries.details: During glacial retreat, a series of proglacial lakes formed in the trough left by the Puget Lobe, including Glacial Lake Russell. By approximately 16,000 BP, the glacier had retreated far enough north that these lakes connected with the Strait of Juan de Fuca, allowing saltwater to re-enter the basin and creating the modern Puget Sound. The resulting fjord system of flooded glacial valleys averages 450 feet in depth, with a maximum depth of 930 feet off Jefferson Point. The deep channels surrounding Vashon Island -- some as deep as the island is high (over 600 feet) -- were carved by subglacial meltwater during the Vashon Stade. This transformation from freshwater lake to marine estuary was the foundational event for the rich marine ecosystem that would later sustain indigenous populations for millennia.

sources.title: Vashon glacier begins to melt and recede from Puget Sound region -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Salmon Colonize Puget Sound Waterways
timeline_entries.description: Pacific salmon colonize the newly formed Puget Sound waterways, likely arriving in two pulses -- from the south via the Chehalis River and from the north through the Strait of Juan de Fuca.
timeline_entries.details: As Puget Sound transitioned from freshwater proglacial lakes to a saltwater estuary, anadromous salmon species began colonizing its rivers and streams approximately 14,900 years ago. Biologists believe colonization occurred in two pulses: an early wave of steelhead and other salmonids arriving from the south via the Chehalis River while the Sound was still freshwater, and a later wave entering from the north after the Strait of Juan de Fuca reopened. Genetic studies show that modern Puget Sound salmon have close relationships to populations on the Olympic Peninsula and Vancouver Island, suggesting the northern route was ultimately more successful. This colonization event established the salmon runs that would become the ecological and cultural cornerstone of the entire region. All five species of Pacific salmon -- Chinook, coho, sockeye, chum, and pink -- eventually established runs in Puget Sound tributaries.

sources.title: Salmon colonize the Puget lowland about 14,900 years ago -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Glacial Retreat Exposes Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: The Vashon glaciation recedes, exposing the landmass that will become Vashon and Maury Islands in the Central Puget Sound Basin.
timeline_entries.details: The Vashon Stade of the Fraser Glaciation, named after the island itself, was the last major glacial advance in the Puget Sound region. As the ice sheet retreated, it carved the deep waterways of Puget Sound and left behind the glacial till that forms the island's terrain. The island's bluffs, ravines, and clay soils are direct artifacts of this glacial history.

timeline_entries.title: Post-Glacial Ecological Succession on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Over several thousand years, Vashon Island transitions from barren glacial till to open lodgepole pine woodland and then to closed mixed-conifer forest, establishing the temperate rainforest ecosystem.
timeline_entries.details: After the ice sheet retreated, the bare glacial landscape of Vashon Island underwent a classic post-glacial ecological succession. Pollen data from regional sites shows that between 16,000 and 15,000 BP, temperatures were about 4 degrees C colder than present and the landscape was largely barren. From about 14,000 to 12,000 BP, lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta) became established in open parkland conditions. Between 12,000 and 10,000 BP, the area developed a wider variety of trees and transitioned to closed forest, with western hemlock (Tsuga heterophylla) and alder joining the mix. By approximately 8,000 BCE, the signature Pacific Northwest species -- Douglas fir, western red cedar, and western hemlock -- had come to dominate, establishing the old-growth temperate rainforest that would blanket the island until 19th-century logging. The entire transition from ice-covered landscape to closed forest took roughly 5,000 to 7,000 years.

sources.title: Vashon glacier begins to melt and recede from Puget Sound region -- HistoryLink.org
Your Woods, Part One -- Vashon-Maury Island Land Trust

timeline_entries.title: First Human Activity on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Evidence of human presence on Vashon Island dates back 10,000 to 12,000 years, among the earliest in the Puget Sound region.
timeline_entries.details: Archaeological evidence suggests that humans were present on Vashon Island shortly after the glacial retreat. These early inhabitants were likely part of broader Paleo-Indian migrations into the Pacific Northwest, taking advantage of the rich marine and terrestrial resources of the newly formed Puget Sound basin.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Island Bluffs, Ravines, and Creek Systems Form
timeline_entries.description: Post-glacial water erosion begins carving the characteristic bluffs, ravines, and creek systems of Vashon Island through the layered glacial deposits of till, outwash sand, and clay.
timeline_entries.details: The retreating Vashon glacier left behind a distinctive layered stratigraphy on the island: Vashon Till (a dense, unsorted mixture of clay, silt, sand, and gravel) capping the surface, underlain by Esperance Sand (porous advance outwash deposited by meltwater streams ahead of the glacier), and below that, Lawton Clay (fine sediment deposited in proglacial lakes). Over the following millennia, surface water exploited the contrast between these layers -- percolating through permeable till and outwash until hitting impermeable clay, then emerging as springs and seeps along the island's coastal bluffs. These seeps and streams carved hundreds of small ravines and creek valleys through the erodible glacial sediments. Shinglemill Creek and Judd Creek cut entirely through the outwash layer. This interplay of geology and hydrology created the island's characteristic landscape of steep coastal bluffs, forested ravines, and spring-fed creeks that would later provide freshwater to both indigenous and settler communities. About 80 percent of the island's drinking water today still comes from the Vashon Advance Outwash aquifer.

sources.title: Going Under Ground: Geology of 'The Rock' -- King County
Geologic Map of the Vashon 7.5' Quadrangle -- USGS

timeline_entries.title: Holocene Climatic Optimum Warms the Puget Sound Region
timeline_entries.description: The Hypsithermal warm period brings temperatures approximately 2 degrees C warmer than present and 45% less precipitation to the Puget Sound region, altering vegetation and shoreline patterns around Vashon Island.
timeline_entries.details: The Holocene Climatic Optimum (also called the Hypsithermal or Altithermal) was a prolonged warm period lasting from roughly 9,500 to 4,500 BP. In the Puget Sound area, temperatures averaged about 2 degrees C warmer than the modern baseline, with approximately 45% less precipitation. The Pacific Northwest initially experienced warm, dry conditions during the Early Holocene (11,700-8,200 years ago), then shifted to cooler and wetter conditions during the Middle Holocene (8,200-4,200 years ago). This warm period would have affected vegetation patterns on Vashon Island, potentially expanding prairie-like openings and oak woodland at the expense of dense conifer forest. The drier conditions also influenced fire regimes and the distribution of plant foods important to early human inhabitants. By the Late Holocene (after 4,200 years ago), the modern cool, wet climate pattern of the Pacific Northwest became established, supporting the dense temperate rainforest for which the region is known.

timeline_entries.title: Shellfish Beds Establish Along Vashon Island Shores
timeline_entries.description: As post-glacial sea levels stabilize and the marine ecosystem matures, productive shellfish beds of clams, oysters, and mussels become established in the intertidal zones around Vashon and Maury Islands.
timeline_entries.details: Following the stabilization of Puget Sound's sea level after post-glacial rebound and eustatic sea-level rise reached a rough equilibrium, productive intertidal shellfish beds became established around the shorelines of Vashon and Maury Islands. The gravelly beaches and protected coves -- particularly in Quartermaster Harbor -- created ideal habitat for native species including littleneck clams, butter clams, horse clams, and the native Olympia oyster. These shellfish beds would become a critical food resource for indigenous peoples for thousands of years, as evidenced by the large shell middens later found at Burton Acres and along Quartermaster Harbor. The Salish Sea as a whole became one of the leading shellfish-producing regions in North America. In some areas of Puget Sound, First Peoples later constructed rock-walled terraces to elevate stretches of intertidal clam beaches -- a form of ancient mariculture known as clam gardens.

sources.title: Gifts from the sea: shellfish as an ecosystem service -- Encyclopedia of Puget Sound

timeline_entries.title: Marpole Cultural Tradition Influences the Puget Sound Region
timeline_entries.description: The Marpole cultural tradition, characterized by social stratification, plank longhouses, intensive salmon preservation, and elaborate carving, flourishes across the Salish Sea region and shapes the ancestral Coast Salish way of life.
timeline_entries.details: The Marpole period (approximately 2,400-1,000 BP) represents a watershed in the cultural development of the peoples who would become the Coast Salish. Named after the c'esna'em (Marpole Midden) site in present-day Vancouver, this cultural tradition was marked by the emergence of clear social classes, permanent winter settlements in cedar-plank longhouses, intensive salmon fishing and preservation, and rich artistic expression including elaborate carvings. Around 400 BCE, a society developed that favored individual acquisition of prestige through peer-elite exchange networks. Archaeological evidence from sites like False Narrows shows that by this period, ascribed (inherited) status was replacing purely achieved status, as evidenced by richly furnished burials of sub-adults. Dentalia shells and copper -- extremely rare and valuable -- appear in high-status graves. By approximately 1000 CE, an elite class had consolidated control over inherited prestige, means of power, and key resources. The Marpole tradition appears to have developed in place rather than arriving from elsewhere, and its cultural patterns form the direct ancestral foundation for the Coast Salish peoples who would inhabit Vashon Island.

sources.title: History of the Coast Salish peoples -- Wikipedia

timeline_entries.title: Permanent Indigenous Villages on Quartermaster Harbor
timeline_entries.description: Archaeological evidence indicates that Native people established permanent year-round villages on Vashon Island at least 2,500 years ago, concentrated along the protected shores of Quartermaster Harbor.
timeline_entries.details: Contrary to the long-held misconception that Vashon Island was used only as a seasonal food-harvesting camp, archaeological evidence demonstrates permanent indigenous habitation dating back at least 2,500 years. The sx̱̌ʷəbabš (Swiftwater People), a band of the Puyallup, established their primary villages along the sheltered shoreline of Quartermaster Harbor, where the combination of protected anchorage, productive shellfish beds, salmon runs, and freshwater streams provided reliable year-round subsistence. By approximately 250 years ago, an estimated 650 Native people lived in six permanent village sites on the island. The permanent villages consisted of communal cedar longhouses averaging 100 feet in length and 20-40 feet wide, housing several extended families, each with their own fire pit. Some villages also included pit houses measuring 40-45 feet square and dug 6-8 feet into the ground for protection from storms. This evidence of permanent settlement was corroborated by Lucy Gerand's testimony in the U.S. Court of Claims in 1927, archaeological excavations, and tribal oral history.

sources.title: Vashon Island's Native People: Navigating Seas of Change -- AASLH
Time&Again - Native People on Vashon Island -- vashonhistory.com

timeline_entries.title: Burton Acres Shell Midden Accumulation
timeline_entries.description: Indigenous inhabitants deposit a large shell midden at Burton Acres on the shore of Quartermaster Harbor over centuries, leaving a rich archaeological record of diet, tools, and daily life.
timeline_entries.details: The Burton Acres Shell Midden, located at a public boat launch on the shore of Quartermaster Harbor, accumulated over centuries as generations of Native inhabitants discarded shells, animal bones, stone tools, fire-cracked rocks, charcoal, and other materials. Shell middens like this one served as communal waste sites and are crucial to understanding the diets and lifestyles of the island's indigenous residents. The site was officially recorded in 1994 by Joan Robinson on behalf of the King County Landmarks Commission. When a severe winter storm in 1995 caused erosion that exposed the midden's contents, a collaborative two-week excavation was organized involving the Burke Museum, University of Washington, King County Landmarks and Heritage Commission, the Puyallup Tribe of Indians, Vashon Park District, and McMurray Middle School, with 375 volunteers participating. The findings were published in 'Vashon Island Archaeology: A View from Burton Acres Shell Midden' (2003), edited by Julie K. Stein and Laura S. Phillips. A separate shell midden discovered on Maury Island in 2009 when a section of Manzanita Beach Road washed away may be connected to a Puyallup fort or village described in 1930s tribal claims court testimony.

sources.title: Vashon Island Archaeology: A View from Burton Acres Shell Midden -- UW Press
A dig on Maury promises a window into the past -- Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber

timeline_entries.title: Coast Salish Cedar Culture on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: The western red cedar, revered as the 'Tree of Life,' becomes the foundation of material culture on Vashon Island, used for longhouses, canoes, clothing, baskets, mats, and medicine.
timeline_entries.details: For thousands of years, the indigenous inhabitants of Vashon Island built their material culture around the western red cedar (Thuja plicata), which they called the 'Tree of Life.' The cedar's straight, lightweight, rot-resistant wood was the primary material for constructing communal longhouses -- some reaching hundreds of feet in length -- and for carving dugout canoes used for fishing, trade, and travel across the waterways of Puget Sound. Canoes were among the most prized possessions, as the heavily timbered landscape made water the primary means of transportation between villages. The inner bark of the cedar was stripped and pounded into a pliable material that was woven into clothing, mats, ropes, and baskets using checkerwork techniques. Cedar roots were also used in basket weaving alongside grasses and other plant fibers. Weavers additionally used the wool of mountain goats and the now-extinct Salish woolly dog to create blankets featuring abstract designs and geometric patterns that served as status markers, ceremonial regalia, and valuable trade items. The Coast Salish approach to cedar harvest was rooted in sustainability, ensuring the trees' survival for future generations.

sources.title: Salish Use of Timber -- University of Washington Tacoma

timeline_entries.title: Coast Salish Seasonal Round of Resource Gathering
timeline_entries.description: The sx̱̌ʷəbabš people of Vashon Island follow an annual seasonal round of food gathering, with salmon fishing, shellfish harvesting, berry gathering, root digging, and hunting timed to natural cycles.
timeline_entries.details: The indigenous inhabitants of Vashon Island organized their subsistence activities around a detailed annual seasonal round, adapted to the natural cycles of the Central Puget Sound. In spring and summer, families moved to temporary camps for harvesting specific resources: camas and other root vegetables were dug, berries (including salal, huckleberry, and salmonberry) were gathered, and shellfish -- clams, oysters, mussels, and crabs -- were harvested from the productive intertidal zones. Summer and fall brought the critical salmon runs, when Chinook, coho, chum, and other species returned to nearby rivers. Although salmon was central, recent archaeological evidence shows that herring, smelt, anchovies, waterfowl, and marine mammals also formed important parts of the diet, countering the 'salmonopia' that long dominated scholarly understanding of Northwest Coast subsistence. In autumn, acorns were collected from the Nisqually Flats and foods were preserved for winter through smoking and drying. Winter was the time for communal life in the longhouses, where social and religious ceremonies took place. The Vashon Heritage Museum's 'Coast Salish Seasonal Round' poster, created for their 2014-15 exhibit and updated in 2023, illustrates this cycle for the native people of Vashon Island and South Puget Sound.

sources.title: Coast Salish Seasonal Round Poster, revised 2023 -- Vashon Heritage Museum

timeline_entries.title: Suquamish Seasonal Use of Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: The Suquamish people, based on the Kitsap Peninsula across the Sound, use Vashon Island as a seasonal encampment for fishing, hunting, and gathering, part of their annual cycle between winter villages and summer resource camps.
timeline_entries.details: While the sx̱̌ʷəbabš maintained permanent year-round villages on Vashon Island, the Suquamish people from the Kitsap Peninsula also utilized the island as part of their seasonal resource-gathering cycle. The Suquamish maintained winter villages at numerous locations including Suquamish, Point Bolin, Poulsbo, Silverdale, Eagle Harbor, and Port Madison. Their most famous winter village was Old Man House (Oleman House), an enormous longhouse estimated at 500-1,000 feet in length that was home to Chief Si'ahl (Seattle) and Chief Kitsap. During warm months, Suquamish families traveled by cedar canoe to temporary camps throughout central Puget Sound, including on Vashon Island, to harvest fish, shellfish, berries, and other seasonal resources. This pattern of shared use of the island by multiple Coast Salish groups reflects the interconnected kinship networks and territorial arrangements characteristic of the broader Puget Sound Salish world. The yearly cycle was divided between food harvesting from temporary warm-weather camps and communal life in substantial winter longhouses for social and religious observances.

sources.title: Delve into the Fascinating History of Vashon Island

timeline_entries.title: Coast Salish Trade Networks Across Puget Sound
timeline_entries.description: Vashon Island's inhabitants participate in extensive waterway-based trade networks connecting Coast Salish peoples across Puget Sound, the Strait of Juan de Fuca, and overland to the Columbia Plateau.
timeline_entries.details: The waterways of the Salish Sea served as major trade routes connecting the Coast Salish peoples in an extensive exchange network. The sx̱̌ʷəbabš of Vashon Island, positioned in the center of Puget Sound, were linked by canoe to neighboring groups including the Puyallup and Nisqually to the south, the Suquamish and Duwamish across the Sound, and more distant peoples throughout the Salish Sea watershed. The kinship-based trade system was facilitated by exogamous marriage -- tribal law required marrying outside one's own group, and marriages between high-ranking families were often arranged at trade centers, creating the kinship ties that made commerce possible. Goods exchanged included ocean products (whale oil, shells, dried fish), mountain resources, camas and wapato roots, berries, cedar products, dentalia shells (used as currency), and rare copper. Overland routes through Snoqualmie Pass connected Puget Sound communities to eastern plateau peoples for exchange of dried salmon, root vegetables, and other goods. All tribes from present-day Olympia to Anacortes spoke dialects of the Puget Sound Salish language, Lushootseed, facilitating communication across these networks.

sources.title: Outside the Ethnographic Box: Native Trade Networks -- The Quartux Journal
Native Americans of Puget Sound -- A Brief History of the First People and Their Cultures -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Guardian Spirit Practices and Winter Ceremonies
timeline_entries.description: Coast Salish spiritual life on Vashon Island centers on the guardian spirit tradition, with vision quests for individual spiritual power and communal winter spirit dance ceremonies held in the longhouses.
timeline_entries.details: The spiritual life of Vashon Island's indigenous inhabitants was rooted in the Coast Salish guardian spirit tradition. Individuals sought personal spirit power through vision quests involving fasting, bathing in cold water, and spending time alone in sacred places. Spirits -- often taking the form of animals such as ravens, bears, woodpeckers, or seals -- conferred specific powers for hunting, healing, leadership, or artistic skill. These spirit encounters were deeply personal, and the songs, dances, and teachings received from the spirit world became part of an individual's identity and family heritage. Winter, when families gathered in the longhouses, was the season for communal spirit dance ceremonies in which members of the community displayed their spirit powers through song and dance on the longhouse floor. The potlatch, another central institution, was a sacred act of giving that maintained social balance, honored ancestors, and reaffirmed community bonds. These ceremonies, along with shamanic healing practices, reinforced the Coast Salish worldview of deep interconnection between the human, animal, and spirit realms. Following European colonization, these practices were suppressed by church and government authorities, but spirit dancing has experienced revival in the modern era.

sources.title: Psychohygienic and therapeutic aspects of the Salish guardian spirit ceremonial -- UBC Library
Indians 101: The Coast Salish vision quest -- Daily Kos

timeline_entries.title: Sqababsh (S'Homamish) Settlement
timeline_entries.description: The sx̌ʷəbabš (Swiftwater People), also known as the Sqababsh or S'Homamish, establish five main village sites on Vashon and Maury Islands.
timeline_entries.details: About 500 years ago, the Sqababsh people settled permanently on the islands, building longhouses at five principal village sites. They were part of the broader Coast Salish cultural group and relied on fishing (particularly salmon), shellfish gathering, hunting, and plant harvesting. The Suquamish and other tribes also used the islands seasonally. Today, many descendants are enrolled members of the Puyallup Tribe of Indians.

sources.title: A Brief History of Vashon Island

timeline_entries.title: Spanish Explorers Approach Puget Sound Entrance
timeline_entries.description: Manuel Quimper sails the Princesa Real into the Strait of Juan de Fuca, discovering Admiralty Inlet -- the entrance to Puget Sound -- but does not enter.
timeline_entries.details: In 1790, Peruvian-born Manuel Quimper was ordered by Francisco de Eliza to explore the Strait of Juan de Fuca aboard the sloop Princesa Real with a crew of forty-one. Quimper charted the strait's interior, discovering the San Juan Islands and many inlets, and was the first European to report seeing Mount Baker. His pilot Juan Carrasco identified the entrance to Admiralty Inlet (which leads to Puget Sound and the waters around Vashon Island), but the expedition did not proceed south into it. Most of Quimper's place names were later overwritten by George Vancouver in 1792, though Port Angeles, Rosario Strait, Quimper Peninsula, and Fidalgo Island retain vestiges of their Spanish origins.

sources.title: Exploration in the Pacific Northwest Before the American Presence -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Spanish Expedition Misses Puget Sound
timeline_entries.description: Jose Maria Narvaez, sailing under Francisco de Eliza, passes by Admiralty Inlet but returns to Nootka Sound without exploring Puget Sound, leaving the waterway for British discovery the following year.
timeline_entries.details: In 1791, Francisco de Eliza ordered a continuation of the exploration of the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Pilot Jose Maria Narvaez aboard the Santa Saturnina passed by Admiralty Inlet (which the Spanish called Ensenada de Caamano), noting it as an entrance to be explored on his return. However, running low on provisions, Narvaez returned directly to Eliza's San Carlos at Port Discovery. By the time he was resupplied, Eliza -- who was ill along with many of his sailors -- decided to return to Nootka Sound. This missed opportunity left Puget Sound and the waters surrounding Vashon Island uncharted by Europeans until George Vancouver's expedition arrived the next year.

sources.title: Spanish expeditions to the Pacific Northwest -- Wikipedia
Exploration in the Pacific Northwest Before the American Presence -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Captain Vancouver Names Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: During British exploratory missions on Puget Sound, Captain George Vancouver names the island after his friend Captain James Vashon of the Royal Navy.
timeline_entries.details: In 1792, Captain George Vancouver led a British expedition surveying the Pacific Northwest coastline. While charting Puget Sound, he named the island after Captain James Vashon, a fellow Royal Navy officer who had served with distinction. Vancouver's expedition produced the first European maps of the area, though indigenous peoples had inhabited the region for millennia.

timeline_entries.title: Peter Puget Surveys Southern Sound Past Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Lieutenant Peter Puget and Master Joseph Whidbey depart HMS Discovery at 4 a.m. in two rowing craft to conduct a week-long survey of the southern Puget Sound, sailing past Vashon Island and charting the waterway's farthest inlets.
timeline_entries.details: On May 20, 1792, Lieutenant Peter Puget and Master Joseph Whidbey departed the HMS Discovery, anchored between Bainbridge and Blake Islands, in two small rowing craft. Over the next six days they surveyed the southern reaches of Puget Sound, passing landmarks now known as Vashon Island, Commencement Bay, Fox Island, and Carr Inlet, and reaching Budd, Case, Eld, Hammersly, and Totten Inlets at the Sound's farthest extremities. Along the way they met and traded with Coast Salish peoples, who knew the waterway as whulge (salt water). Puget observed signs of a recent smallpox epidemic among the indigenous residents. On May 29, Vancouver honored Puget's work by naming the southern portion of the waterway 'Puget's Sound,' a name that eventually expanded to encompass the entire body of water.

sources.title: Explorer George Vancouver names Puget's Sound for naval officer Peter Puget on May 29, 1792 -- HistoryLink.org
George Vancouver begins British survey of Puget Sound on May 19, 1792 -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Hudson's Bay Company Establishes Fort Nisqually
timeline_entries.description: The Hudson's Bay Company builds Fort Nisqually on southern Puget Sound, establishing the first European settlement in the region and a fur trade hub within sight of the waters around Vashon Island.
timeline_entries.details: In the spring of 1833, Chief Trader Archibald McDonald established Fort Nisqually for the Hudson's Bay Company near the mouth of Sequalitchew Creek on the plains north of the Nisqually River delta, in present-day DuPont, Washington. It was the first European settlement on Puget Sound. The HBC crew built cedar houses, a store, and protective walls, trading guns, blankets, and clothing with Coast Salish peoples for beaver, otter, and other furs. The fort served as a principal port for domestic and foreign trade and later expanded into agriculture through the Puget Sound Agricultural Company subsidiary. Fort Nisqually's presence drew European and American attention to the broader Puget Sound region, including the islands, and operated until 1869.

sources.title: Hudson's Bay Company builds Fort Nisqually in spring 1833 -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Lt. Wilkes Names Maury Island
timeline_entries.description: Lt. Charles Wilkes of the United States Exploring Expedition surveys Puget Sound and names Maury Island after crew member William A. Maury.
timeline_entries.details: The Wilkes Expedition (1838-1842) was the first U.S. naval expedition to survey the Pacific Northwest. When Lt. Wilkes charted the waters around Vashon Island, he named the smaller adjacent island after William A. Maury, a member of his crew. At this time, Vashon and Maury Islands were separated at high tide but connected by a natural sandbar at low tide.

timeline_entries.title: Wilkes Expedition Names Quartermaster Harbor Features
timeline_entries.description: During the U.S. Exploring Expedition, Lt. Charles Wilkes names Quartermaster Harbor and nearly all of Vashon-Maury Island's coastal points after quartermasters on his voyage.
timeline_entries.details: When the United States Exploring Expedition (1838-1842) under Lt. Charles Wilkes surveyed Puget Sound in 1841, Wilkes produced the first American charts of the Vashon-Maury Island area. In addition to naming Maury Island after crew member William A. Maury, Wilkes named Quartermaster Harbor -- the sheltered harbor between Vashon and Maury Islands -- and nearly all of the islands' coastal points (including Point Beals, Point Heyer, and others) after quartermasters serving on the expedition. These names reflected American claims to the region, which was then jointly occupied by the United States and Britain under the 1818 convention, and many of these place names persist to the present day.

sources.title: Delve into the Fascinating History of Vashon Island

timeline_entries.title: Donation Land Claim Act Opens Vashon Island to Settlement
timeline_entries.description: Congress passes the Donation Land Claim Act, granting up to 640 acres of Oregon Territory land to married settlers, providing the legal mechanism under which Vashon Island will be claimed starting in the 1860s.
timeline_entries.details: The Donation Land Claim Act, which took effect September 27, 1850, granted 320 acres of federal land to white male citizens who resided on and cultivated the land for four years, and 640 acres to married couples. Authored by Samuel Royal Thurston, it was designed to encourage settlement of the Oregon Territory, which then included present-day Washington. The act explicitly excluded Black and Hawaiian settlers. By the time it expired in 1855, approximately 30,000 white immigrants had entered Oregon Territory, claiming 2.5 million acres. Land on Vashon Island did not begin to be claimed under this act until the mid-1860s, after the Medicine Creek Treaty had removed indigenous land claims and the S'Homamish people had been displaced. The act provided the legal framework for Pope and Talbot's 1864 logging claim and Arthur Phinney's 592-acre claim the same year.

sources.title: Donation Land Claim Act, spur to American settlement of Oregon Territory, takes effect on September 27, 1850 -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Logging Begins on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Commercial logging operations begin on Vashon Island, marking the start of European-American economic activity on the island.
timeline_entries.details: Logging was the first major industry on Vashon Island, exploiting the dense old-growth forests of Douglas fir, western red cedar, and hemlock that covered the island. The timber was transported by water to mills around Puget Sound. This activity preceded permanent European-American settlement by over a decade.

timeline_entries.title: Early Logging Camps Operate on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Transient logging camps with crews of about eight men each cut old-growth timber along Vashon Island's shorelines, dragging logs by ox-team to the beach where they are boomed and towed to mainland mills.
timeline_entries.details: From the early 1850s through the mid-1860s, before permanent settlement, Vashon Island was worked by small logging crews who operated camps near the shoreline. A typical camp consisted of a bunkhouse and a cook shack, with an ox-team skid road leading down to the beach. An estimated 200 million board feet of timber remained on the island as of the mid-1880s. The logging camps lacked any semblance of family life -- most workers were single men who migrated from camp to camp. The dense forests of Douglas fir, western red cedar, and hemlock were the island's first commercially exploited resource, and the cost of overland transport confined all operations to within a mile or two of the water's edge. This pre-settlement logging was the only significant non-indigenous economic activity on the island for over a decade.

timeline_entries.title: Medicine Creek Treaty and S'Homamish Removal
timeline_entries.description: The Medicine Creek Treaty cedes indigenous land claims to the U.S. government. By 1855-1856, the S'Homamish people are relocated to Fox Island.
timeline_entries.details: The Medicine Creek Treaty of 1854, negotiated by Territorial Governor Isaac Stevens, required indigenous peoples to cede their lands in exchange for reservation territory and fishing rights. The Sqababsh/S'Homamish of Vashon Island were removed to Fox Island by 1855-1856, ending thousands of years of continuous habitation. This displacement opened the island to European-American homesteading.

sources.title: A Brief History of Vashon Island

timeline_entries.title: Puget Sound Indian War and Fox Island Internment
timeline_entries.description: The Puget Sound War erupts following the Treaty of Medicine Creek; nearly 5,000 indigenous people, including the S'Homamish from Vashon Island, are forcibly interned on Fox Island under devastating conditions.
timeline_entries.details: In October 1855, armed conflict broke out between U.S. forces and Nisqually, Muckleshoot, Puyallup, and Klickitat warriors angered by the Treaty of Medicine Creek's unfair terms. To separate 'non-hostile' indigenous people from combatants, Acting Governor Mason ordered the collection and disarming of all Native peoples east of Puget Sound. Nearly 5,000 men, women, and children -- including the S'Homamish formerly of Vashon Island -- were forcibly interned on Fox Island under guard of John Swan. Exposed to winter weather with no shelter and inadequate food, over one-third of the internees fell ill by May 1856. On January 26, 1856, a coalition of tribes attacked the settlement of Seattle in the war's most dramatic battle. The war ended after Nisqually Chief Leschi retreated east; he was later captured, controversially convicted of murder, and hanged in 1858. Leschi was posthumously exonerated in 2004.

timeline_entries.title: Pope and Talbot File First Land Claim on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Andrew J. Pope and William C. Talbot of the Puget Mill Company at Port Gamble claim 80 acres on the west side of Vashon Island for logging, marking the first non-indigenous land claim on the island.
timeline_entries.details: On August 1, 1864, Andrew J. Pope and William C. Talbot -- principals in the Puget Mill Company at Port Gamble -- filed a claim for 80 acres on the west side of Vashon Island under the Donation Land Claim Act. This was the first formal land claim on the island. Pope and Talbot, both from Maine sawmill families, had built their Port Gamble mill in 1853 and were expanding their timber operations throughout the Sound. The Vashon claim was used for logging, with timber dragged to the shore, boomed, and towed by tug to their mill. The same year, Arthur Phinney made claims totaling 592 acres in the area that would later become the town of Vashon.

timeline_entries.title: First European-American Settler on Vashon
timeline_entries.description: Mathew Bridges files the first homestead claim on Vashon Island, becoming the island's first permanent European-American settler.
timeline_entries.details: Mathew Bridges arrived on Vashon Island and filed a land claim, beginning the era of European-American settlement. In the years following, other homesteaders followed, drawn by available land and the island's natural resources. The early settlers relied on fishing and logging as primary occupations.

timeline_entries.title: Chinese Fishing Community Established at Manzanita
timeline_entries.description: Chinese settlers establish a thriving fishing colony locally called 'Hong Kong' at Manzanita on Maury Island, among the first non-indigenous communities on Vashon-Maury Island, until the anti-Chinese expulsions of November 1885.
timeline_entries.details: In the mid-1870s, Chinese settlers established a fishing colony at Manzanita on the southwest shore of Maury Island -- well before any organized European-American community existed on the island. Vashon's first historian, Oliver Van Olinda, described 'a very large and busy colony, with a wide wharf extending over four hundred feet along the shore,' where the principal occupation was fishing and fish-drying, with thousands of tons of dried fish shipped from the site. Using enormous seine nets measuring 900 feet long and 240 feet deep, the Chinese fishermen worked Elliott Bay, Port Madison, and local waters. It is likely the first Chinese fishing boat on Puget Sound was built at Manzanita. The community was destroyed in November 1885 when anti-Chinese violence erupted across the region; on November 3, Tacoma forcibly expelled all its Chinese residents in what became known as 'The Tacoma Method,' and the Manzanita colony simultaneously disappeared.

sources.title: Time and Again: From Vashon's early Chinese settlers to today -- Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber

timeline_entries.title: Sherman Family Becomes First Permanent Settlers
timeline_entries.description: Salmon and Eliza Sherman, along with the Price and Gilman families, settle along Quartermaster Harbor, taking shelter in an abandoned logger's shack they nickname 'Fort Necessity' -- the first permanent family settlement on Vashon Island.
timeline_entries.details: In 1877, Salmon Sherman (born 1836 in New York) and his wife Eliza (born 1846 in Wisconsin), lured from Minnesota by the promise of free land, arrived at Vashon Island with their relatives the Prices and the Gilmans. They settled along present-day Quartermaster Drive, taking shelter in an abandoned logger's shack they dubbed 'Fort Necessity.' While Mathew Bridges had filed a homestead claim in 1865, the Shermans are considered the first permanent family settlers, establishing a continuous presence that persists to the present day -- descendants of the Sherman family, now in their sixth generation, still live on the island. S.D. Sherman later rowed mail from Tacoma to Quartermaster Harbor before converting a lifeboat into the schooner Old Black Joe to provide the island's first semi-regular ferry service.

sources.title: Gene Sherman, 'a man of history,' leaves a legacy -- Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber

timeline_entries.title: First County Roads Established on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: King County establishes its first official roads on Vashon Island -- Roads No. 116 and 117 (now SW Cemetery Road and SW Bank Road) -- connecting the island's interior settlements to the coast.
timeline_entries.details: In 1883, King County formally established its first roads on Vashon Island. Road No. 116 (today's SW Cemetery Road) was petitioned by Edwin Broadway and others, running from the center of the island to the Ellisport dock. Road No. 117 (today's SW Bank Road) was petitioned by T.D. Soper and others, leading from the island's center to the brickyard and post office at Vashon Landing. Road No. 118 (today's Vashon Highway SW) was petitioned by Mason Holmes and others, running south from Road No. 117. Maury Island pioneer Bill Rendall described the roads of this era as 'hardly justified the name, as the greater part of it was only a little wider than a wagon.' These primitive tracks through heavy timber were nonetheless essential for connecting the island's scattered homesteads and enabling overland commerce.

sources.title: First County Roads & Docks -- My Vashon Island Blog

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Post Office Opens
timeline_entries.description: The island's first post office opens on April 12, 1883, with Samuel C. Herriott as postmaster, establishing an official U.S. government presence and regularizing mail delivery on Vashon Island.
timeline_entries.details: On April 12, 1883, the Vashon Post Office -- the island's first -- opened with Samuel C. Herriott appointed as postmaster. Before this, S.D. Sherman had rowed mail from Tacoma to the Quartermaster Harbor area by hand, later delivering it aboard his converted lifeboat Old Black Joe. The post office formalized the island's connection to the broader communication network and signaled growing federal recognition of the settlement. By 1887, Captain John Vanderhoef's steamer Iola held the mail contract for the east side of Vashon-Maury, picking up and delivering mail at Adelaide, Maury, Chautauqua, and Vashon Landing. Additional post offices followed at Chautauqua and Maury in 1888, reflecting the island's growing population and multiple community centers.

sources.title: Vashon Island beginnings: Vashon Post Office opens on April 12, 1883 -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Methodist Church Organized -- First Church on Vashon
timeline_entries.description: Rev. Albert Atwood organizes the first Methodist class on Vashon Island on April 4, 1884, and a log church is built the following year -- the first church building on the island.
timeline_entries.details: On April 4, 1884, at the request of island residents, John N. Dennison of Seattle's Methodist Church sent Rev. Albert Atwood to organize a Methodist class on Vashon Island. As early as 1881, a log schoolhouse on the island had provided a shared worship space for both Baptists and Methodists. The cornerstone of the Vashon Methodist Church was laid in 1885 on the Ward property, and the building was constructed from hand-hewn logs. At the dedication, the sermon topic was 'Happy is that people whose God is the Lord.' The church was recognized as the first on Vashon Island. Early conditions were rugged -- the organist walked two miles each way to play for services -- but the church quickly became central to community life. A Presbyterian church and Baptist church at Center followed in subsequent years.

sources.title: VUMC History -- Vashon United Methodist Church

timeline_entries.title: First Ferry Service Established
timeline_entries.description: S.D. Sherman purchases a lifeboat and refits it as a schooner to provide semi-regular ferry service to Vashon Island.
timeline_entries.details: By the 1880s, enough settlers had arrived that regular transportation to the mainland became essential. S.D. Sherman converted a lifeboat into a small schooner to provide the first semi-regular service. This modest beginning eventually led to established ferry routes at both the north and south ends of the island, which in turn attracted more homesteaders. Early settlers also built the first school, stores, and crude roads during this period.

timeline_entries.title: First Chautauqua Assembly on Puget Sound Held on Vashon
timeline_entries.description: On August 3, 1885, the first Chautauqua assembly on Puget Sound is held at Dilworth Point on Vashon Island, launching a cultural education movement that will draw thousands to the island for the next three decades.
timeline_entries.details: On August 3, 1885, the first Chautauqua on Puget Sound was held at Dilworth Point on Vashon Island, organized by Rev. R.B. Dilworth, who had been active in the original Chautauqua assembly in New York since 1874. Named after Chautauqua, New York, the movement offered summertime lectures, discussions, and cultural activities in a resort atmosphere. The inaugural program included devotional services, Sunday school, German language instruction, roundtable discussions, and music; round-trip fare from Seattle on the steamer Zephyr cost 75 cents. In 1888, the Puget Sound Chautauqua Assembly chose Tramp Harbor on Vashon as its permanent home, platting Chautauqua Beach -- the first town platted on the island -- with streets named for writers like Bryant, Emerson, and Hawthorne. The site grew to 600 acres with a 1,200-seat pavilion, hotel, dock, and hundreds of cottages, hosting speakers reportedly including Mark Twain and Theodore Roosevelt before declining in the 1920s.

sources.title: Chautauqua comes to Vashon Island on August 3, 1885 -- HistoryLink.org

timeline_entries.title: Steamer Iola Begins Regular Service to Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Captain John Vanderhoef takes command of the steamer Iola and establishes six weekly round trips between Tacoma, Seattle, and Vashon Island landings, creating the island's first reliable Mosquito Fleet connection.
timeline_entries.details: In June 1887, Captain John F. Vanderhoef became master and agent of the steamer Iola, a small steamship built at Hammersley Inlet in 1885. Vanderhoef rebuilt the cabins to serve as living quarters for himself and his wife, and established a schedule of six round trips per week serving Vashon Island: Monday, Wednesday, and Friday via East Passage (stopping at Adelaide, Maury, Chautauqua, and Vashon Landing) and Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday via Colvos Passage on the west side. This was a major step up from S.D. Sherman's earlier converted-lifeboat service. The Iola held the mail contract for the east side of Vashon-Maury Island and was part of the broader 'Mosquito Fleet' -- the armada of small steamships that connected Puget Sound communities from the 1880s through the 1920s, serving an estimated 350 or more destinations. By 1889, Vanderhoef had concentrated entirely on the Vashon Island route.

timeline_entries.title: Brick Manufacturing Boom at Quartermaster Harbor
timeline_entries.description: Brickyards proliferate around Quartermaster Harbor, exploiting the island's accessible clay deposits; at peak operation there are five yards employing 200 men, with the Bleeker Brickyard at Burton being the largest.
timeline_entries.details: Easily accessible clay deposits along Vashon Island's shorelines made clay-mining and brick-making one of the island's most significant early industries. By the late 1880s, as many as ten to twelve brickyards had operated on the island at various times, with five concentrated around Quartermaster Harbor employing approximately 200 men. The Bleeker Brickyard at Burton was the largest; the steam barge 'Molly Bleeker' ferried bricks to Tacoma and doubled as living quarters for the Bleeker family. Lucian Cook ran a separate brickyard on Quartermaster Harbor, bought the steamer Estella, and ran it between Tacoma and the harbor to transport bricks and workmen. In 1889, Cook had six barges built for hauling bricks and purchased the steamer Seaside as a towboat. The Fairfowld Brick Yard alone employed 100 men, with most bricks used in Tacoma for buildings and streets. The industry declined sharply after the 1893 financial panic devastated Puget Sound construction markets.

timeline_entries.title: Frank Gorsuch Opens First Store in the Town of Vashon
timeline_entries.description: Frank Gorsuch builds and opens the first store at the crossroads that will become the town of Vashon, establishing the commercial nucleus that eventually supersedes Center and Burton as the island's primary hub.
timeline_entries.details: In 1890, Frank Gorsuch built a general store at the crossroads formed by the island's earliest farm roads, where the Livesley, Blackburn, and Ward properties met near the north end ferry route. The store carried everything a frontier community needed -- spices, coffee, tobacco, oils, feed, hardware, kerosene, groceries, cloth, sewing supplies, and clothing. Island pioneer Ira Thompson recalled that 'although overland travel was tough and the mud deep, Gorsuch was soon doing business with people throughout the Island.' The building, which still stands, was later sold to Fred and Henry Weiss (who renamed it Weiss Bros. General Merchandise in 1913) and then became Vashon Hardware Company in 1929. The structure was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2000. Gorsuch's store at this location effectively founded the town of Vashon, which gradually eclipsed Center and Burton as the island's commercial heart once automobiles and the north-end ferry dock shifted transportation patterns.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon College Opens at Burton
timeline_entries.description: Miles Hatch spearheads the founding of Vashon College near Burton as a non-denominational Christian institution; its first building, Old Main, is four stories with 46 rooms, and the school fields teams that compete against the University of Washington.
timeline_entries.details: In 1892, Vashon College opened near the town of Burton on Quartermaster Harbor. Miles Hatch, an early island entrepreneur who founded and named Burton after his birthplace of Burton Township, Illinois, led the effort and donated the hilltop campus land. A.C. Jones was hired as the first president. The first building, Old Main, was an impressive four-story structure with 46 rooms serving as classrooms, offices, a dining hall, and student residences. A three-story commercial building for 90 male students was added in 1894, expanded in 1898, and in 1901 the Armory -- the largest drill hall in Washington state at the time -- was constructed. The college offered classical and scientific four-year programs, a pharmacy school, conservatory of music, and school of commerce. Assuring parents that 'there was not a drop of alcohol on the island,' the school required daily chapel attendance. The football team competed against the University of Washington and Tacoma Athletic Club. A fire in 1910 dealt a fatal blow; the campus sat largely empty until a second fire in 1930 led to its demolition.

timeline_entries.title: Great Fire and Financial Panic Devastate the Island
timeline_entries.description: In August 1893, a massive wildfire sweeps through the center of Vashon Island while a nationwide financial panic simultaneously collapses the Puget Sound economy, destroying homes and devastating island industries.
timeline_entries.details: August 1893 brought a devastating one-two blow to Vashon Island. A wildfire that began in a logged-off area near the site of the present high school (where the first sawmill had been located) raged for two days and nights. Nearly a hundred volunteers fought desperately with shovels, hoes, and rakes to save the new Baptist Church and the Presbyterian Church at Center, and the Fuller store across the street. With flames within two hundred yards of Center, the wind shifted north on the evening of the second day, allowing firefighters to gain control. Many families lost their homes and property. Compounding the disaster, a nationwide financial panic had already hit the Puget Sound region hard -- 14 Tacoma banks failed, and the construction market that sustained the island's brick industry collapsed. The combined effect stalled the island's development for several years, though the cleared land ultimately became available for farming as the community rebuilt.

timeline_entries.title: Chautauqua Assembly Established at Tramp Harbor
timeline_entries.description: The Puget Sound Chautauqua Assembly selects Tramp Harbor on Vashon Island as its permanent home, creating a 600-acre cultural and educational resort with a 1,200-seat pavilion.
timeline_entries.details: After the first Puget Sound Chautauqua was held at Dilworth Point on Vashon Island in 1885, the assembly incorporated in 1887 and selected Tramp Harbor for a permanent site in 1888. Islanders McClintock Ellis, Fuller, and Judd donated 115 acres. The site grew to 600 acres with two miles of shoreline, a hotel, dozens of cottages, parks, a steamer dock, and a 1,200-seat pavilion. Roads were named after writers (Bryant, Emerson, Hawthorne) and trees (Alder, Fir, Cedar). Programs included lectures, concerts, clambakes, art instruction, Biblical sermons, and talks on science and temperance. Speakers included Mark Twain and Theodore Roosevelt. Round-trip steamer fare from Seattle cost 75 cents. The site was renamed Ellisport in 1912, but the movement declined with the rise of electricity, telephones, and radio, vanishing by the 1920s.

sources.title: Chautauqua comes to Vashon Island on August 3, 1885 (HistoryLink.org)

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Island Brick Industry Supplies Seattle and Tacoma
timeline_entries.description: Eight or more brickyards operate on Vashon and Maury Islands, employing over 200 men and supplying bricks for the rebuilding of Seattle after the Great Fire of 1889.
timeline_entries.details: In 1891, a group of Tacoma businessmen including M.F. Hatch of Vashon Island formed The Puget Sound Drydock Company. They purchased an unfinished dry dock originally built for Port Townsend (whose real estate market had collapsed) and towed it from Port Hadlock to the sheltered cove at the mouth of Quartermaster Harbor. The drydock measured 325 feet long by 102 feet wide — one of the largest on the Pacific Coast. Peter Manson, noting the facility could 'dock a ton of boats,' named the new village Dockton. By June 1892, the dock employed more than 80 workers. Alfred J. Stuckey served as superintendent until 1909. John A. Martinolich, a Croatian-born shipbuilder who arrived in 1896, founded his own yard in 1904 and became known as the 'King of Purse Seiners' for his fishing boat designs. Many workers came from the Dalmatian Coast; Croatian surnames were so common that Dockton was nicknamed 'Ichville.' Workers lived in a large three-story hotel; managers lived in 'Piano Row' — the only island homes large enough to hold a piano.

timeline_entries.title: Japanese American Strawberry Farming Begins
timeline_entries.description: Japanese Americans begin growing strawberries on Vashon Island, establishing an industry that will define the island's agriculture for 50 years.
timeline_entries.details: Starting around 1890, Japanese American families began cultivating strawberries on Vashon Island. The island's mild maritime climate and rich glacial soils proved ideal for berry production. This industry grew to become a major part of the island economy and a defining cultural feature of Vashon life until the forced internment during WWII.

timeline_entries.title: Sawmills and Steamer Routes Serve the Island Economy
timeline_entries.description: Multiple sawmills operate on Vashon Island while daily steamer service on the Sophia connects mills, brickyards, and docks to Tacoma markets.
timeline_entries.details: By 1890, M.F. Hatch operated a sawmill at Assembly Point on the Burton Peninsula, and the steamer Sophia began making daily trips to Tacoma, stopping at Sherman's Dock, Hatch's Sawmill, Dockton Dry Dock, Bleeker's brickyard, and Burrow's brickyard. By 1892, the Sophia ran three daily trips with fares of fifteen cents round trip. Six mills, a gravel bunker, a brickyard, a cannery, and a creamery were in operation. Frances Sherman ran a sawmill in Paradise Valley and won a contract to supply lumber for the Luna Park amusement park at Alki Point. The Steen Mill, founded in 1902, later joined by the Fuller, Pankratz, Covey, and Vashon Island mill companies, continued the logging tradition. Helmar Steen built a logging railroad along what is now Cove Road, and his mill provided his home with an early luxury: electric light.

sources.title: Town of Vashon 1890-1921 (My Vashon Island Blog)

timeline_entries.title: First Telephone Lines on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Vashon Island's first telephone line -- a half-mile acoustic wire between a newspaper office and the J.T. Thompson household -- is strung in 1891, with organized telephone service arriving via the Farmers Mutual Company in 1904.
timeline_entries.details: In 1891, the first telephone line on Vashon Island ran half a mile between the local newspaper office and the J.T. Thompson household -- little more than an acoustic wire system. Legend holds that islanders J. Jacobs and Mr. Webber had already rigged a tin-can-and-string system between their homes in 1892. The push for real telephone service gained momentum when the Tacoma Times reported in 1903 that islanders were 'very enthusiastic about establishing communication.' In 1904, the Farmers Mutual Independent Telephone Company secured a franchise and set up an exchange in the town of Vashon serving the north part of the island. Lines were strung on trees rather than poles. Service was connected to Seattle in June 1904 and to Tacoma in July, though the undersea cable gave persistent trouble -- by 1907, 80 of 125 customers signed a petition threatening to cancel service if the cable was not fixed within two months.

sources.title: History of Vashon's Independent Telephone Companies (My Vashon Island Blog)
Early Vashon Town 1890-1914 (My Vashon Island Blog)

timeline_entries.title: Dockton Drydock Built
timeline_entries.description: A drydock is constructed at Dockton on Maury Island, the only facility of its kind on Puget Sound at the time.
timeline_entries.details: The drydock at Dockton was a significant industrial facility, serving the maritime industry of Puget Sound. Located on the southwestern shore of Maury Island, it represented the island's participation in the broader regional economy beyond agriculture and logging. The facility attracted workers and contributed to the growth of the Dockton community.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon College Founded at Burton
timeline_entries.description: Miles Hatch and community leaders establish Vashon College near Burton as a non-denominational Christian co-educational school, with Oliver Scott Van Olinda joining the founding faculty.
timeline_entries.details: In 1892, Miles F. Hatch spearheaded the founding of Vashon College as a non-denominational Christian college for 'young people of both sexes of good moral character.' A.C. Jones was hired as the first president, and construction began on land west of Burton donated by Hatch. The first building, Old Main, was a four-story structure with 46 rooms serving as classrooms, offices, dining hall, and residences. A three-story commercial building was added in 1894, and the Armory -- then the largest drill hall in the state -- was added in 1901. Oliver Scott Van Olinda, the island's first historian, taught stenography and typing on the founding faculty and also edited the weekly Vashon Island Press. Tuition for a 15-week semester in 1896 cost $22.50. The college could accommodate 200 students. Fires in 1906 and 1910 damaged the campus, and a final fire in 1930 led to the remaining buildings being razed.

sources.title: Time & Again: Learning at Vashon College and Vashon 101 (Vashon Beachcomber)

timeline_entries.title: Burton Emerges as the Island's Social and Commercial Center
timeline_entries.description: Burton, founded by Miles and Mrs. M.F. Hatch at Quartermaster Harbor, becomes the dominant town on Vashon Island with the college, daily steamer service, the post office, churches, and commercial enterprises.
timeline_entries.details: In 1892, Miles Hatch built a two-story store at the west end of the Burton Peninsula, and his wife named the settlement after her birthplace in England (Burton-In-Kendall). Hatch also claimed much of the Burton Peninsula as his homestead, started Vashon College, developed the Mileta Farm dairy, and ran a sawmill at Assembly Point. With daily steamer service to Tacoma and its college, Burton quickly surpassed other island communities. The Baptist Missionary Children's Home opened in 1895, and the First Baptist Church of Burton opened in 1897. Residents exchanged used magazines on a roadside log, inspiring the Women's Club to found the Burton Rental Library in 1916. Burton remained the island's major town until automobiles, improved roads, and the north-end ferry dock shifted the commercial center to Vashon town in the 1920s.

sources.title: Vashon Library, King County Library System (HistoryLink.org)

timeline_entries.title: The Panic of 1893 and Great Fire Strike Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: A nationwide financial collapse and a devastating wildfire in August 1893 combine to halt Vashon Island's boom-era growth, destroying homes and collapsing the brick and lumber markets.
timeline_entries.details: In 1893, Vashon Island was struck by twin calamities. The national Panic of 1893 caused bank failures across Puget Sound -- 14 of Tacoma's 21 banks collapsed -- crushing demand for the island's brick and lumber products and depressing agricultural prices. Then in August 1893, a wildfire broke out in the logged-off area near the first sawmill (near the present high school site) and raged for two days and nights. Nearly a hundred volunteers fought desperately with shovels, hoes, and rakes to save the Baptist and Presbyterian Churches at Center and the Fuller store. With the flames within two hundred yards of Center, a wind shift on the evening of the second day allowed firefighters to gain control. The Tacoma Yacht Club at Manzanita went bankrupt in 1894 as a direct result of the depression. Population growth on the island slowed significantly for the remainder of the decade.

sources.title: Panic of 1893: Seattle's First Great Depression (HistoryLink.org)

timeline_entries.title: Commercial Strawberry Cultivation Begins
timeline_entries.description: John Cage Gorsuch plants the first commercial strawberry operation on Vashon Island, harvesting 6,120 pounds per acre by 1896 and launching the island's signature agricultural industry.
timeline_entries.details: John Cage Gorsuch likely started the first commercial strawberry operation on Vashon Island in the early 1890s, planting strawberries on his property just north of Vashon town. By 1896, Gorsuch was harvesting 6,120 pounds of strawberries from each of his three acres. Other farmers quickly followed suit, drawn by the island's mild maritime climate and rich glacial soils. By 1901, 15,000 crates were shipped off island, and by 1909, the number had grown to 120,000 crates. The Vashon Island News proclaimed Vashon the 'Home of the Big Red Strawberry.' This commercial success laid the foundation for the Japanese American farming community that would come to dominate strawberry production in the following decades.

sources.title: Island Festivals (Bruce Haulman and Terry Donnelly)

timeline_entries.title: Burton Masonic Hall Built by Woodmen of the World
timeline_entries.description: The Woodmen of the World fraternal order constructs a two-story lodge hall at Burton, the island's first fraternal building, which still stands as a King County landmark.
timeline_entries.details: In 1894, the Woodmen of the World -- a fraternal benefit society -- commissioned local carpenter Howard C. Stone to build a two-story gable-front lodge building in Burton overlooking Quartermaster Harbor. The first floor housed commercial uses while the upstairs was reserved for lodge meetings and social gatherings. This was the island's first fraternal building, reflecting Burton's status as the social center of the island. In 1925, Mark P. Waterman Lodge #177, Free and Accepted Masons, took over the building. The hall is now a designated King County landmark and represents the fraternal organizations that shaped island community life in the 1890s.

sources.title: King County Landmarks: Burton Masonic Hall (1894) (HistoryLink.org)

timeline_entries.title: Opium Washes Ashore on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Resident J.E. Mace discovers bags of smuggled opium on a Vashon Island beach, revealing the island's position along Pacific Northwest maritime smuggling routes.
timeline_entries.details: In the spring of 1895, pioneer J.E. Mace found a heavy canvas sack on the beach during his regular Sunday beachcombing. Inside were small tin cans of opium, part of the extensive maritime smuggling trade between Victoria, British Columbia -- then home to 13 opium refining factories -- and Puget Sound ports. Mace showed the substance to a well-traveled neighbor named Hopkins, who identified it as opium. Mace buried it on neighbor Asa Start's property, left a map with his wife, and traveled to Seattle to report his find to the Customs Office. Government agents had already been on the island posing as land buyers. By court order of Judge Hanford in June 1895, Mace received $175 for turning in the opium, which sold for $564. When Mace found a second bag weeks later, he fell under suspicion, and agents used his son Ed's cap to try to lead tracking dogs to a larger cache, but nothing was found.

timeline_entries.title: Harrington-Beall Greenhouse Company Established
timeline_entries.description: The Harrington-Beall Greenhouse Company grows from an 1888 start into the nation's largest grower of roses and an orchid establishment of international renown, becoming the island's largest employer.
timeline_entries.details: The Harrington-Beall Greenhouse Company began on a 23-acre site southeast of Vashon's business center in 1888 and operated for 101 years. Partnered with Tom Beall Jr (grandson of founder Lewis Cass Beall Sr), the business grew into a 150,000-square-foot operation with over 50 greenhouses constructed with window glass imported from Belgium. By 1923, it was described as 'without a doubt the largest industry on the Island,' employing 25 to 30 men year-round. The complex contained 59 greenhouses spanning 100 years of greenhouse technology evolution. During World War II, rare orchids from England were shipped to Vashon for safekeeping. Operations were relocated to Bogota, Colombia in the 1970s, and the property was sold in 1989. The district, including the 1885 Hilen Harrington Log House, is a designated King County landmark.
