timeline_entries.title: Island Population Triples: 944 to 2,810
timeline_entries.description: The population of Vashon-Maury Island nearly triples in twenty years, growing from 944 residents in 1900 to 2,423 in 1910 (a 156% increase) and reaching 2,810 by 1920.
timeline_entries.details: The early 20th century brought the fastest population growth in Vashon Island's history. The 1900 census recorded 944 residents; by 1910 the population had surged 156% to 2,423, driven by expanding agriculture, the arrival of Japanese American farmers, and the island's growing reputation as both a farming community and recreational retreat. By the 1920 census, the population reached 2,810 across nine precincts: Burton, Cove, Dockton, Dolphin, Island, Lisabuela, Maury, Quartermaster, and Vashon. Home ownership rates dropped from 76.4% in 1900 to 66.1% by 1920, reflecting the influx of young single men on the 'Wageworker's Frontier' and rising land costs. Growth slowed sharply during the 1920s agricultural depression, and by 1940 the population had increased only 11% above the 1920 level.

timeline_entries.title: Spring Beach Resort and Summer Tourism Flourish
timeline_entries.description: The Miramar Lodge opens at Spring Beach in 1905, and by 1915 over 8,000 visitors arrive from Tacoma each summer season, making Vashon Island a popular Puget Sound resort destination.
timeline_entries.details: In 1905, the Miramar Lodge was built at the Spring Beach resort on the southwest shore of Vashon Island, less than three miles from Tacoma's Point Defiance Park. The lodge served as the resort manager's residence, dining room, general store, and post office. A small boat called the Tourist ran back and forth from Point Defiance. By 1915, over 8,000 visitors per summer arrived from Tacoma. The resort offered 50 cabins and many tents for rent, along with hiking trails, boat rentals, clambakes, and fishing. A water fountain shot into the air and landed in an agate-lined pool. Other resorts included the Magnolia Beach community (platted in 1902 by Tacoma resident Charles A. Cook) and the Luseta Beach Resort. Advertisements promised visitors could 'escape the noxious vapors and immoral influences of a crowded city.'

sources.title: Time and Again: Inn at Magnolia Beach attracted early Vashon tourists (Vashon Beachcomber)
Private Steamer Docks (My Vashon Island Blog)

timeline_entries.title: First Paved Road and Automobile Era Transform the Island
timeline_entries.description: The first automobiles arrive on Vashon Island in 1907, and by 1921 the island's first paved road -- a cement highway from Center to the Heights ferry dock -- becomes the first paved road on any Puget Sound island.
timeline_entries.details: The first automobiles reached Vashon Island in 1907, beginning a transformation that historian O.S. Van Olinda called 'the most powerful influence' on island life alongside the telephone. The Vashon Island Auto Club formed to advocate for road improvements and signage. The first auto ferry arrived in 1916, connecting Portage to Des Moines. In 1921, using the Donahue Act (which split road costs between property owners and the state), residents paved the road from Center to the Heights ferry dock with cement laid by Kaiser Corporation -- the first paved road on a Puget Sound island. Named the Leif Hamilton Scenic Highway after a King County councilman, this concrete highway soon linked to other paved roads traversing the island. The Portage-Des Moines ferry route was abandoned in 1922 in favor of the more convenient Vashon Heights-Harper route, and the island's center of gravity shifted from south-facing Burton to the north end.

sources.title: Town of Vashon 1890-1921 (My Vashon Island Blog)
Town of Vashon 1922-1960 (My Vashon Island Blog)
Road Map Vashon-Maury Islands (Barry Lawrence Ruderman Antique Maps)

timeline_entries.title: First Strawberry Festival Held on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: The inaugural Vashon Island Strawberry Festival celebrates the island's booming berry industry, with 120,000 crates shipped off-island that year.
timeline_entries.details: By 1909, strawberry production on Vashon Island had grown from John Cage Gorsuch's pioneering three acres in the 1890s to an industry shipping 120,000 crates annually. The Vashon Island News proclaimed the island the 'Home of the Big Red Strawberry,' and the first Strawberry Festival was organized to celebrate. The festival became annual in 1912, sponsored by the Vashon Federation of Clubs. By the 1910s and 1920s, Japanese American farmers had come to dominate strawberry production. In 1923, 101-year-old Melissa Jaynes was crowned Vashon's first Strawberry Queen. The festival was suspended during WWII and changed names several times (Peach Festival in 1946, Harvest Festival, Island Festival) before reverting to the Strawberry Festival name. It continues today as the island's most anticipated annual event, drawing tens of thousands.

sources.title: Island Festivals (Bruce Haulman and Terry Donnelly, vashonhistory.com)

timeline_entries.title: Denichiro Mukai's Strawberry Barreling Innovation
timeline_entries.description: Denichiro Mukai arrives on Vashon Island and develops a renowned method for barreling fresh strawberries that concentrates flavor and moisture.
timeline_entries.details: Denichiro ('B.D.') Mukai arrived on Vashon Island around 1910 and began farming strawberries. Unable to own land himself due to the 1921 Washington State Alien Land Law, he purchased 40 acres in the name of his 15-year-old American-born son, Masahiro ('Masa'), in 1926. The Cold Process Fruit Barreling Plant was established in 1927 as the Vashon Island Packing Company ('VIPCO'). The patented cold process packed berries into wooden barrels at a 2:1 ratio of fruit to sugar (300 lbs. strawberries to 150 lbs. sugar per barrel), then shipped them to Spokane Street Cold Storage in Seattle for freezing. This was the first commercial frozen berry operation in the United States. By the 1930s, the farm employed over 400 workers annually, shipped 200 tons of strawberries per year, and housed 250 seasonal workers in an on-site bunkhouse. The farm remained profitable through the Great Depression. In 1934, B.D. retired to Japan and Masa, age 23, a Washington State University engineering graduate, took over. In 1939, with anti-Japanese sentiment rising, Masa renamed the business 'Vashon Island Packing Company' to reduce its Japanese-sounding profile.

sources.title: Delve into the Fascinating History of Vashon Island

timeline_entries.title: Puget Mill Company Logs 10 Square Miles of the Island
timeline_entries.description: The Puget Mill Company logs 10 sections (10 square miles) of Vashon-Maury Island's 33 total square miles between 1910 and 1915, transforming the island's landscape from forest to open farmland.
timeline_entries.details: Between 1910 and 1915, the Puget Mill Company conducted intensive industrial-scale logging operations, clearing roughly 30% of Vashon-Maury Island's total land area. This massive deforestation, combined with earlier logging and fires -- including a 1922 blaze that burned the width of the south end from Tahlequah northward for two miles -- gave the island a clearcut appearance. A few large trees were spared in the deepest ravines and can still be seen today. The removal of the old-growth forest permanently altered the island's ecology and directly enabled its transition to an agricultural economy, particularly strawberry farming. By 1994, a WSU Extension forestry assessment found that over 60% of the island had been reforested with second-growth timber.

timeline_entries.title: Tombolo Connects Vashon and Maury Islands
timeline_entries.description: A permanent land connection (tombolo) is constructed between Vashon Island and Maury Island, replacing the tidal sandbar.
timeline_entries.details: Before 1913, Vashon and Maury Islands were only connected during low tide by a natural sandbar. The construction of a permanent tombolo created a year-round land bridge between the two islands, fundamentally changing transportation and settlement patterns. This engineering project unified what had been two separate island communities.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Island Electrification Begins at Ellisport
timeline_entries.description: G.A. Collins builds a steam electric generating plant at Ellisport, bringing the first electric lights to Vashon Island; Governor Lister inaugurates the system in November 1913.
timeline_entries.details: The Vashon Electric Co. received a franchise to construct a steam electric plant on the island, and G.A. Collins built the facility at Ellisport. The system was inaugurated on November 24, 1913, with Governor Ernest Lister pressing the button. The generator charged 15 cents per kilowatt hour. Power lines were extended to Dockton in 1917. The Vashon Electric Railroad Company was also formed with a 40-year franchise to build an electric railroad from the north to south end of the island, with $50,000 pledged by island farmers, though the railroad was never completed. In 1923, Puget Sound Power & Light Co. purchased the holdings of Washington Coast Utilities, including Vashon's electric and telephone systems, connecting the island to hydroelectric power from the Dieringer plant between Sumner and Auburn.

sources.title: Town of Vashon 1890-1921 (My Vashon Island Blog)

timeline_entries.title: First Auto Ferry to Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: The King County Ferry System begins auto ferry service with the M.V. Vashon running between Des Moines and Portage.
timeline_entries.details: The arrival of the automobile ferry in 1916 marked a transformative moment for Vashon Island. The M.V. Vashon, operated by the King County Ferry System, connected the island to the mainland at Des Moines via the Portage landing. This made the island far more accessible and accelerated its development as both a farming community and a retreat from urban Seattle.

timeline_entries.title: Camp Sealth Founded by Camp Fire Girls
timeline_entries.description: Ruth A. Brown founds Camp Sealth, the first permanent resident camp for girls in Washington State, on Blake Island in 1920; it moves to a 150-acre site on Vashon Island's southwest corner in 1921.
timeline_entries.details: Camp Sealth was founded in 1920 by Ruth A. Brown as the first permanent resident camp for girls in Washington State, beginning on Blake Island for its inaugural season. In 1921, Camp Fire leaders found an attractive site on the southwest corner of Vashon Island -- 180 acres of former Luseta Beach Resort land with five streams, one mile of beach, an orchard, wharf, and seventeen cottages. A campaign raised $8,585 to purchase the land. Contractor E.J. Rounds volunteered his services, Kiwanis members helped carry lumber and erect posts, and Camp Fire Girls applied paint and hammers to the cottages. On June 26, 1921, seventy-five girls arrived on the Virginia IV to start the first summer at the Vashon site. A south-end forest fire burned part of the camp in 1922, and campers helped fight the blaze. The camp has expanded to nearly 400 acres and has operated for over 100 continuous summers.

sources.title: Camp Sealth -- Memories we Cherish (Camp Fire Girls Camp Histories)

timeline_entries.title: Mukai Cold Process Fruit Barreling Plant Built
timeline_entries.description: The Mukai family purchases 40 acres in their American-born son Masa's name and builds the Cold Process Fruit Barreling Plant, employing over 400 seasonal workers and shipping 200 tons of strawberries annually.
timeline_entries.details: Unable to own land under Washington's 1921 Alien Land Law, Denichiro 'B.D.' Mukai and his wife purchased 40 acres in 1926 in the name of their American-born son Masahiro 'Masa' Mukai (born 1911 on Vashon Island). They built a one-story wood-frame barreling plant designed by Masa and constructed by local contractor Deb Harrington. Strawberries were packed into wooden barrels using a 2-to-1 ratio of berries to sugar -- 300 pounds of strawberries and 150 pounds of sugar per barrel -- then sent to Spokane Street Cold Storage in Seattle for freezing. In 1928, the family built a Craftsman bungalow with Colonial Revival details, and B.D.'s second wife Kuni created a formal Japanese stroll garden. Throughout the Depression years, the farm prospered, employing over 400 workers annually, including Native Americans who traveled from Vancouver Island by canoe. The company was renamed the Vashon Island Packing Company (VIPCO) in 1938. The plant became a King County landmark in 1993 and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1994.

sources.title: Mukai Cold Process Fruit Barrelling Plant (Wikipedia)

timeline_entries.title: The Great Depression Stalls Island Growth
timeline_entries.description: The agricultural depression of the late 1920s and the Great Depression of the 1930s collapse farming and chicken ranching on Vashon Island, leaving many islanders dependent on government construction jobs.
timeline_entries.details: An agricultural depression in the late 1920s foreshadowed harder times to come. Decreased demand, falling prices, and increased costs hit the island's farming and chicken ranching industries, and the population began to decline before the national Depression even began. During the 1930s, many islanders were unemployed and dependent on government-created construction jobs. New home construction slowed, and the use of seasonal pickers increased as farm families grew smaller and jobs became scarce. Depression-era homes were built with minimal skills from materials obtained at little or no cost -- the Schwartz-Bell house (1930), a pole-frame building sheathed in cedar log slabs, exemplifies this approach. A devastating fire struck the town of Vashon in the middle of the Depression; most buildings were rebuilt within six weeks, with only two remaining unrestored. By 1940, the population had grown only 11% above the 1920 level of 2,810.

sources.title: Town of Vashon 1922-1960 (My Vashon Island Blog)
Time and Again: A History of Housing on Vashon (Vashon Beachcomber)

timeline_entries.title: Filipino Farmworkers Face Anti-Filipino Backlash
timeline_entries.description: Filipino farmworkers on Vashon Island face harassment, death threats, and violence from white workers fearful of losing jobs in the first year of the Great Depression.
timeline_entries.details: In the spring of 1930, roughly 50 Filipino workers were expected on Vashon Island to work the fruit ranges around Burton. But as the Great Depression set in, Filipino farmworkers -- already paid roughly half of white workers' wages -- became targets of hateful treatment. Dynamite was exploded outside their living quarters, their jobs were limited to those unwanted by others, and white farm owners who hired Filipinos received death threats. On the night of May 12, 1930, Filipino farmworker Louis Modaranga, employed at the Steen Mill box factory in Ellisport, was attacked by four white men. Modaranga (possibly Pedro Modaranga in census records, a 29-year-old fruit-farm laborer from the Philippines) was charged with felony assault despite testimony from King County Deputy Sheriff F.J. Shattuck that the assault was provoked. None of the white attackers were arrested. The King County prosecutor said Modaranga was unjustly held. Similar anti-Filipino violence occurred in nearby Kent and Auburn.

sources.title: Filipino workers face backlash on Vashon Island (HistoryLink.org)

timeline_entries.title: Japanese American Internment
timeline_entries.description: Vashon Island's Japanese American community is forcibly relocated to internment camps under Executive Order 9066, ending 50 years of strawberry farming.
timeline_entries.details: Following the attack on Pearl Harbor and Executive Order 9066, the Japanese American families of Vashon Island were forced to leave their homes and farms for internment camps. This devastated the island's strawberry industry, which had been a cornerstone of the local economy for half a century. Most families lost their land and property. Few returned after the war, and the agricultural landscape of the island was permanently altered.

timeline_entries.title: Day of Exile: Vashon Japanese Americans Forcibly Removed
timeline_entries.description: On May 16, 1942, 111 Japanese Americans are gathered at Ober Park under armed guard and forcibly removed from Vashon Island, ending decades of community life.
timeline_entries.details: On May 16, 1942, U.S. armed soldiers rounded up 111 islanders of Japanese ancestry at Ober Park in the town of Vashon. Before the war, 132 Japanese Americans lived in 31 households on the island; 17 had already departed for college, military service, or jobs elsewhere. The remaining residents were shipped to Seattle and forced onto rail cars with blackened windows. They were sent first to the Pinedale Assembly Center in the California desert, a temporary holding facility, then transferred to Tule Lake Relocation Center. From Tule Lake, families were eventually scattered across seven of the nine West Coast concentration camps, including Heart Mountain in Wyoming and Minidoka in Idaho. The day is now commemorated annually on Vashon as the 'Day of Exile.'

sources.title: Ceremony will commemorate Day of Exile at Ober Park - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber
Man remembers family, island struggles 74 years after Japanese internment - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber

timeline_entries.title: Mukai Family Self-Exiles to Oregon Before Internment Order
timeline_entries.description: Tipped off by a military friend, Masahiro (Masa) Mukai moves his family from Vashon to Dead Ox Flat, Oregon, becoming voluntary evacuees who avoid the internment camps.
timeline_entries.details: Masa Mukai received advance warning of the coming internment from a friend in the U.S. military. Rather than wait for the forced removal, he left the family's strawberry farm and cold-process fruit barreling business in the hands of trusted neighbors and moved his family -- wife Chiyeko, mother Kuni, and son Milton -- to Dead Ox Flat (also known as Dead Ox Flats) in eastern Oregon, where Chiyeko had relatives. Although they avoided imprisonment, they encountered hostility and prejudice nonetheless. Masa purchased 100 acres and farmed row crops, even inventing his own seed harvester. The four Mukai family members were the only Vashon Japanese Americans to avoid the concentration camps.

sources.title: Chapter 3 - Overcoming Adversity: Masa Mukai's Remarkable Story - Discover Nikkei

timeline_entries.title: Army Units Stationed on Vashon for Puget Sound Defense
timeline_entries.description: U.S. Army units are deployed to Vashon Island as part of the Puget Sound defense system, with headquarters at Center School.
timeline_entries.details: In early 1942, Army units were assigned to Vashon as part of the broader Puget Sound defense system following the attack on Pearl Harbor and fears of Japanese naval attacks on the Pacific coast. The Army established its headquarters at the Center School, located at the southeast corner of Vashon Highway and S.W. 204th Street. This military presence marked the beginning of decades of defense installations on the island, which would later include Nike missile sites during the Cold War.

sources.title: Time&Again: Vestiges of Vashon's military past remain - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber

timeline_entries.title: Collapse of Vashon Strawberry Industry After Internment
timeline_entries.description: The forced removal of Japanese American farmers devastates Vashon's strawberry industry, which had been a cornerstone of the island economy for over 50 years.
timeline_entries.details: Before the internment, Japanese American families were the backbone of Vashon's strawberry industry, which had thrived since the 1890s. When 111 Japanese Americans were forcibly removed in May 1942, their farms were abandoned or taken over by others. The specialized knowledge, labor networks, and farming infrastructure built over decades were lost almost overnight. The Mukai cold-process fruit barreling plant, which had been a significant agricultural enterprise, ceased operations. After the war, only a fraction of the Japanese American farmers returned, and the industry never recovered its former scale. This agricultural collapse contributed to the island's economic transition away from farming toward other industries and eventually toward its identity as a bedroom community and arts enclave.

sources.title: Time and Again: Roots and Branches of Island Agriculture - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber
Digging into Japanese American Farming History on Vashon Island - Discover Nikkei

timeline_entries.title: Yoneichi Matsuda Joins 442nd Regimental Combat Team
timeline_entries.description: Yoneichi Matsuda, from a Vashon Island strawberry farming family, volunteers from Heart Mountain internment camp to serve in the U.S. Army's legendary 442nd Regimental Combat Team.
timeline_entries.details: While interned at Heart Mountain War Relocation Center in Wyoming, Yoneichi Matsuda -- whose family had farmed strawberries on Vashon Island since 1927 -- volunteered to serve in the U.S. Army's 442nd Regimental Combat Team. The 442nd was composed almost entirely of Japanese American men and became the most decorated unit for its size and length of service in U.S. military history, fighting in the European theater against Nazi forces. His sister Mary Matsuda later described his departure from camp as one of the saddest days of the family's life. Mary herself would eventually leave the camps to join the U.S. Cadet Nurse Corps.

sources.title: Book Review: Looking Like The Enemy - Discover Nikkei

timeline_entries.title: Partial Return of Japanese Americans to Vashon
timeline_entries.description: Only about one-third of Vashon's exiled Japanese Americans return to the island after the war; many find their property lost or destroyed.
timeline_entries.details: After the war ended and the camps were closed, only about one-third of the 111 Japanese Americans forcibly removed from Vashon on May 16, 1942, returned to the island. Many families had lost all their belongings except what they could carry in two suitcases. Some learned that homes belonging to Japanese residents had been burned during the war. Political hostility toward returning Japanese Americans in Washington State discouraged others from coming back. The Sakaharas, for example, chose not to return and rebuilt their lives elsewhere. The Mukai family did return from self-exile in Oregon, reopened their home and garden, resumed strawberry farming, and restarted their cold-process fruit barreling plant. The once-thriving Japanese American farming community on Vashon was permanently diminished.

sources.title: 1945 - When Once Exiled, Imprisoned Families Returned Home - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber
Japanese family farm reflects a troubled time in our history - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber

timeline_entries.title: Washington State Ferries Begins Service
timeline_entries.description: Washington State Ferries takes over island ferry service on June 1, 1951, replacing the private Vashon Ferry System.
timeline_entries.details: After the private Vashon Ferry System operated for three years, Washington State Ferries assumed control of the route on June 1, 1951. This transition brought the island into the state transportation network. Around this time, state officials proposed connecting Vashon-Maury Island to the mainland with bridges, but islanders increasingly opposed the idea, fearing it would destroy the island's rural character and invite urban sprawl.

timeline_entries.title: Nike Missile Base S-61 Established on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: The U.S. Army establishes Nike missile site S-61 on Vashon Island as part of a twelve-site defense ring protecting Seattle during the Cold War.
timeline_entries.details: In 1953, as Cold War fears of Soviet atomic attacks on Seattle grew, the U.S. Army deployed the 513th Air Defense Battalion's Battery C ('Charlie Battery') on Vashon with anti-aircraft guns. Between 1956 and 1957, the government purchased land through eminent domain for three sites: Sunrise Ridge (administration and fire control), Paradise Ridge (missile launch area with underground silos), and Oakwood Terrace (housing). The base was designated S-61 in the twelve-site Metropolitan Defense Ring surrounding Seattle. Initially armed with Nike Ajax missiles, the site was upgraded to Nike Hercules in June 1960 -- one of only three Seattle-area bases to receive the more powerful missiles. The 433rd Anti-Aircraft Artillery Missile Battalion, Battery A, operated the base until its closure in 1974. The Sunrise Ridge site, ironically, had been a strawberry farm owned by the Matsumoto family before the government condemned the land.

sources.title: The Nike Base - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Bridge Proposal Defeated in State Legislature
timeline_entries.description: A bill to fund a bridge connecting Vashon Island to the mainland dies in the Washington State Senate after Lt. Governor John Cherberg's procedural ruling, effectively killing the most serious bridge proposal in island history.
timeline_entries.details: By the late 1950s, the Washington Toll Bridge Authority had advanced an ambitious plan to build a cross-sound highway: a floating bridge from Fauntleroy to Vashon (which would have been the largest floating structure ever built at 11,666 feet), a superhighway across the island, and a suspension bridge across Colvos Passage to the Kitsap Peninsula. Engineers estimated 3-4 million vehicle crossings in the first year, with construction costs of approximately $100 million. On March 12, 1959, after the state legislature struggled for nearly three months during a second special session, the House passed the appropriations bill. However, Lt. Governor John Cherberg, who served as Senate president, ruled that the House bill had broadened the original scope and must return to committee. A vote to override Cherberg's ruling failed 21 to 28. The bill died in the Highways Committee and the bridge was never built. Opponents included the Pilots Association, the Port of Tacoma, and Eastern Washington legislators, along with a growing number of Vashon residents who feared becoming 'another Mercer Island.'

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Allied Arts Becomes Oldest Private Nonprofit Arts Organization in Washington
timeline_entries.description: Vashon Allied Arts (formerly the Vashon Arts League, founded 1949) receives its 501(c)(3) nonprofit status, becoming the oldest private nonprofit community arts organization in Washington State.
timeline_entries.details: The Vashon arts community traces its institutional roots to 1949, when island artists Fred Eernisse, Norman Edson, and Art Hansen formed the Vashon Arts League to show art created by islanders. After moving through several temporary homes -- the Lisabuela schoolhouse and the Cove Road Church -- the organization was revitalized by Shirley Speidel and others who found a home in the old Boy Scout Cabin at Ober Park. In 1966, the organization received 501(c)(3) status under the name Vashon Associated Arts, making it the oldest private nonprofit community arts organization in the state. The organization would eventually become Vashon Center for the Arts (VCA), growing into the island's largest nonprofit with programs in visual arts, performing arts, arts education, and dance.

sources.title: VCA History - Vashon Center for the Arts

timeline_entries.title: Counterculture Influx Transforms Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: An estimated 200-700 counterculture migrants settle on Vashon Island during the Boeing Bust era, fundamentally reshaping the island's cultural identity.
timeline_entries.details: The Boeing Bust and economic downturn of the early 1970s created an opening for counterculture and alternative-lifestyle individuals to find affordable housing on Vashon. As island families left to seek employment, small abandoned farms became available at low rents. By 1971, an estimated 200-700 'hippies' lived on the island alongside about 6,500 existing residents. A planned Memorial Day Weekend Rock Festival in Paradise Valley in 1970 sparked community tensions -- three loggers held down and forcibly cut the hair of 17-year-old Tony Grant, shops posted 'No Shoes, No Shirts, No Service' signs, and some called for an armed 'Sheriff's Deputy Auxiliary' to control the supposed invasion. Over 700 people attended a hearing and shouted down the armed patrol idea. Cannabis cultivation became widespread, earning Vashon the lasting nickname 'Weed Island' for the high-quality 'Vashon Gold' strain sold across the West Coast. Despite early friction, the counterculture movement permanently transformed Vashon from a quiet agricultural community into the progressive, arts-oriented enclave celebrated by the bumper sticker 'Keep Vashon Weird.'

timeline_entries.title: The Bike in the Tree: Vashon's Accidental Landmark
timeline_entries.description: A child's red bicycle left in the woods by Don Puz in 1954 is gradually absorbed by a growing fir tree, becoming one of Vashon Island's most iconic and quirky landmarks.
timeline_entries.details: In 1954, the Puz family suffered a devastating house fire that killed Don Puz's father and destroyed all their possessions. In true 'Vashon fashion,' neighbors donated household items to help the family rebuild, including a red bicycle for young Don. At some point, Don left the bicycle leaning against a small fir tree in the woods near what is now Vashon Highway SW and SW 204th Street, behind the building called Sound Food. Over the decades, the tree grew around the bicycle, gradually absorbing it into the trunk. The sight became a beloved local attraction and the inspiration for Berkeley Breathed's children's book 'Red Ranger Came Calling.' A widely circulated but false internet story claims the bike belonged to a boy who left it to fight in World War I and never returned. Jeff Ammon, who owned Vashon's only bike shop, maintained the landmark by replacing handlebars and wheels when vandals stripped them. Don Puz, who grew up to become a King County Sheriff's deputy, confirmed his ownership when he returned to see the tree decades later.

timeline_entries.title: Island Resists Bridge Construction
timeline_entries.description: Vashon Island residents successfully resist repeated proposals to build a fixed bridge to the mainland, preserving the island's rural isolation.
timeline_entries.details: Over several decades, various proposals to connect Vashon Island to the mainland via bridge were debated and ultimately rejected. Islanders recognized that a bridge would fundamentally alter the character of their community, making it a suburb of Seattle rather than a distinct island community. The ferry-dependent isolation became a defining and deliberately preserved feature of island life.

timeline_entries.title: K2 Corporation Founded on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Brothers Bill and Don Kirschner found K2 Corporation on Vashon Island, pioneering fiberglass ski technology that revolutionizes the ski industry.
timeline_entries.details: Bill Kirschner, a University of Washington engineering graduate, had been experimenting with fiberglass skis in his grandfather Otto's garage on Vashon Island since the 1950s while running Kirschner Manufacturing, which produced veterinary splints and research cages from fiberglass. After years of prototypes that broke apart during testing at Crystal Mountain, Bill perfected a wet-wrap fiberglass process in 1961. In 1962, he and brother Don formally founded K2 -- named for both the world's second-highest mountain and the two Kirschner brothers. Only 250 pairs shipped in 1964, but by 1967 the business was separated from Kirschner Manufacturing, and by 1968, K2 was selling 21,000 pairs annually with 83 employees. The company's racing program brought instant success with U.S. Ski Team adoption. At its peak, the Vashon factory employed approximately 750 islanders, making K2 the largest private employer on the island.

timeline_entries.title: K2 Sports Manufacturing on Vashon
timeline_entries.description: K2 Sports operates a major ski and sporting goods manufacturing facility on Vashon Island before eventually moving production to China.
timeline_entries.details: K2 Sports was one of Vashon Island's largest employers, manufacturing skis and other sporting equipment on the island for decades. The company's eventual decision to move manufacturing to China represented a significant economic shift for the island, as it lost one of its few major industrial employers. Similarly, Seattle's Best Coffee operated a roastery on the island until it was acquired by Starbucks and the operation was closed.

timeline_entries.title: Stewart Brothers Coffee Opens Roastery on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Jim Stewart moves his coffee roasting operation to Vashon Island, establishing the roastery that would become Seattle's Best Coffee.
timeline_entries.details: In 1982, coffee entrepreneur Jim Stewart moved his roasting facilities to Vashon Island, purchasing a historic building constructed from old-growth island fir in the town of Vashon. The building featured an expansive covered porch, high ceilings, wooden floors, and an underground cellar perfect for storing rare coffee beans. Stewart had started in the coffee business in 1969 with the Wet Whisker ice cream and coffee shop on Whidbey Island. After winning first place in a regional coffee tasting competition judged by the area's top chefs, the company changed its name from Stewart Brothers Coffee to Seattle's Best Coffee (SBC). The Vashon roastery became the birthplace and production center for one of the Pacific Northwest's most iconic coffee brands. Starbucks acquired SBC in July 2003 and closed the Vashon facility on October 23, 2003, moving production to their Kent, Washington roastery. The historic building was later reopened as The Vashon Island Coffee Roasterie, still roasting coffee with the original equipment.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Island Farmers Market Established
timeline_entries.description: The Vashon Island Growers Association (VIGA) establishes a farmers market, sparking a revival of sustainable agriculture on the island.
timeline_entries.details: In the mid-1980s, a group of islanders formed the Vashon Island Growers Association (VIGA) with the goal of creating on-island farming jobs. They started a small farmers market near the Post Office and joined Washington Tilth, a statewide organization promoting local organic agriculture. By 1990, the market moved to its current site at the Village Green. In 1998, VIGA received a grant to build a permanent shed structure, and the following year led a community-wide effort that raised over $200,000 to purchase the Village Green property. The market became a catalyst for the fifth stage of island agricultural history: a revival of sustainable and organic farming methods after decades of agricultural decline following the WWII internment and postwar economic shifts. VIGA also developed educational programs including a horticulture curriculum at Vashon High School. The Saturday market now runs April through October, featuring farm produce, local crafts, prepared foods, and live music.

sources.title: Time and Again: Roots and Branches of Island Agriculture - Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber

timeline_entries.title: Vashon-Maury Island Land Trust Founded
timeline_entries.description: Islanders establish the Vashon-Maury Island Land Trust to preserve natural areas, beginning with the purchase of Whispering Firs Bog.
timeline_entries.details: In 1989, a dedicated group of islanders concerned about preserving Vashon's natural character informally organized to purchase Whispering Firs Bog, a fragile and unique wetland ecosystem near the Episcopal Church. The organization formally incorporated in 1990 as the Vashon-Maury Island Land Trust. Since its founding, the Land Trust has permanently protected over 2,000 acres of land, built 10 miles of public trails, and preserved key natural features including salmon-bearing streams, major ponds, diverse forests, and shoreline areas. Notable preserves include Shinglemill Creek, Judd Creek, Fisher Pond, and Christensen Pond. The Land Trust also permanently protected the remaining 12 acres of the historic Matsuda Farm, linking conservation with Japanese American heritage preservation. The organization launched programs like 'Seven over Seventy' to conserve large private holdings and 'The Four Creeks Campaign' to protect the island's major watersheds. Vashon carries half of all King County's shorelines, giving the Land Trust an outsized role in Puget Sound aquatic habitat protection.

timeline_entries.title: Mukai Farm Listed on National Register of Historic Places
timeline_entries.description: The Mukai Farm and Garden on Vashon Island is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, preserving one of the last intact pre-WWII Japanese American farmsteads in America.
timeline_entries.details: The Mukai House, Garden, and Barreling Plant (5 acres remaining of the original 40+) was designated a King County Landmark in 1993 — the first site associated with Japanese American history to receive that designation. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1994. Masahiro Mukai died in 1999. In 2000, the nonprofit Island Landmarks purchased the property with $500,000 in public funds from King County, the National Park Service, and the State of Washington. The garden, designed by Kuni Mukai in 1928, survives as a rare intact example of Japanese stroll garden design in the Pacific Northwest — the only known Japanese stroll garden of that era designed by a woman. Ongoing restoration of the Barreling Plant, supported by a $150,000 NEH Challenge Grant, aims to convert it into a Vashon Food Hub. In 2021, King County Executive held an honorary street designation ceremony naming a road 'Mukai Way.'

timeline_entries.title: Glacier Northwest Gravel Mine Controversy on Maury Island
timeline_entries.description: A 13-year battle over Glacier Northwest's proposed gravel mine expansion on Maury Island ends when King County purchases the 200-acre site for $36 million, creating a new county park.
timeline_entries.details: Glacier Northwest had operated a gravel mine on the southern tip of Maury Island since the 1940s. In 1998, the company announced plans to dramatically expand operations to approximately 7.5 million tons of gravel per year, including construction of a 305-foot pier for barge transport. The proposal ignited fierce community opposition led by Preserve Our Islands, a grassroots organization founded by Sharon Nelson. Environmental concerns included arsenic contamination from decades of ASARCO smelter fallout, threats to an aquatic reserve surrounding the site (one of only four in Washington), potential harm to endangered Southern Resident orca whales from barge noise, and drinking water contamination. Over 500 islanders rallied at Gold Beach in one of Vashon's largest protests. After Glacier Northwest won multiple legal battles and began pier construction, a federal judge blocked further work in 2009, ruling the Army Corps of Engineers had acted 'arbitrarily and capriciously' in violation of the Endangered Species Act. On December 30, 2010, King County Executive Dow Constantine completed the purchase of the site for $36 million, funded through the Asarco settlement, Conservation Futures fund, and a CalPortland lease extension. The parcel became a county park, protecting a mile of shoreline and over 200 acres of madrone forest adjacent to the 320-acre Maury Island Regional Marine Park.

timeline_entries.title: K2 Sports Moves Manufacturing Off Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: K2 Sports relocates manufacturing from Vashon Island to Guangdong, China in 2001, and moves its business offices to Seattle's Industrial District in 2006, ending over 40 years on the island.
timeline_entries.details: In 2001, facing pressure to remain financially competitive in a globalizing market, K2 Sports moved its manufacturing operations from Vashon Island to Guangdong, China. At its peak, the Vashon factory had employed approximately 750 local people, making K2 one of the island's largest private employers. On June 22, 2006, K2 announced it was also relocating its business offices from Vashon Island to Seattle's Industrial District. The original factory building on Vashon Highway remained vacant for over a decade until its sale in July 2018 to Sound Properties, LLC. The departure of K2 represented a significant economic blow to Vashon, accelerating the island's transition from a place with industrial employment to primarily a residential and arts community.

timeline_entries.title: Mary Matsuda Gruenewald Publishes 'Looking Like the Enemy'
timeline_entries.description: At age 80, former Vashon Island resident Mary Matsuda Gruenewald publishes her memoir of wartime internment, preserving the story of the island's Japanese American community.
timeline_entries.details: Mary Matsuda Gruenewald, born on Vashon Island in 1925 to Japanese immigrant strawberry farmers Heisuke and Mitsuno Matsuda, published 'Looking Like the Enemy: My Story of Imprisonment in Japanese American Internment Camps' in 2005. The memoir recounts her family's forced removal from Vashon on May 16, 1942, and her experiences at the Pinedale Assembly Center, Tule Lake, and Heart Mountain camps. It also tells the story of her brother Yoneichi's service with the 442nd Regimental Combat Team and her own enlistment in the U.S. Cadet Nurse Corps. David Guterson, author of 'Snow Falling on Cedars,' described it as 'a painfully honest narrative of imprisonment.' A Young Readers edition was published in 2010. In 2017, Vashon Island High School retroactively awarded Gruenewald the diploma she was denied when internment cut short her education. She died on February 11, 2021, at age 96. The memoir is now widely used in university and high school curricula.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Island COVID-19 Community Response
timeline_entries.description: Vashon Island mounts a volunteer-led pandemic response that achieves the lowest COVID-19 case rate in King County, earning national recognition as a model for rural communities.
timeline_entries.details: When the Seattle area became the nation's first COVID-19 hotspot in March 2020, Vashon Island faced unique vulnerabilities: an older-than-average population (median age 53), no hospital, limited clinic capacity, and ferry-dependent access to testing and medical care. Unemployment on the island quickly reached 22%, with four out of ten businesses going dark. The Vashon Medical Reserve Corps (VMRC) and VashonBePrepared launched an integrated response program that included community education (200+ situation reports, bilingual English-Spanish materials), free SARS-CoV-2 testing (7,500+ PCR tests), rapid contact tracing (560 index cases investigated), and an aggressive vaccination campaign (19,000+ doses delivered in partnership with Vashon Pharmacy). A community fundraising drive raised $325,000, later supplemented by $413,000 in government reimbursements. Volunteers contributed over 31,500 hours, and the relief fund subsidized over 4,400 bags of groceries and 28,000 meals. Over the first 22 months, Vashon achieved the lowest cumulative COVID-19 case rate in King County: 11.2 cases per 1,000 residents versus the countywide 49.6. The New York Times recognized VMRC's approach as a model for rural and tribal communities. A peer-reviewed study published in PLOS ONE confirmed the response's effectiveness.

timeline_entries.title: Black Ball Line Sold to Washington State
timeline_entries.description: The State of Washington purchased the Puget Sound Navigation Company (Black Ball Line) fleet from Captain Alexander Peabody for $4.9 million, creating Washington State Ferries.
timeline_entries.details: Captain Alexander Peabody's Black Ball Line had long been the primary ferry operator on Puget Sound, including routes to Vashon Island. After years of contentious disputes over fares and subsidies, and a crippling 1947 strike that left island communities stranded, the state legislature authorized the purchase. The acquisition transformed ferry service from a private monopoly into a public utility, fundamentally changing how island communities related to the state government.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Island Independent Ferry District Formed
timeline_entries.description: Following the devastating 1947 Black Ball Line ferry strike that left Vashon Island isolated, residents formed an independent ferry district to ensure reliable transportation service.
timeline_entries.details: The 1947 strike by the Inlandboatmen's Union against the Black Ball Line left Vashon Island residents unable to commute to work or obtain supplies for weeks. The crisis galvanized the community to take control of its transportation future, leading to the formation of the Vashon Island Ferry District in 1948. This grassroots response demonstrated the island community's capacity for self-governance and foreshadowed the eventual state takeover of ferry operations in 1951.

timeline_entries.title: Tahlequah-Point Defiance Ferry Route Established
timeline_entries.description: Washington State Ferries established the Tahlequah-Point Defiance route, providing a direct connection between southern Vashon Island and Tacoma/Pierce County.
timeline_entries.details: The Tahlequah-Point Defiance route became one of two primary ferry connections for Vashon Island (the other being the northern route to Fauntleroy in West Seattle). The southern route provided access to Tacoma and the Kitsap Peninsula via Point Defiance. Together, the two routes defined the island's unique position as equidistant between Seattle and Tacoma, accessible to both yet truly part of neither.

timeline_entries.title: Cross-Sound Bridge Proposal Debated
timeline_entries.description: The Cross-Sound Bridge Bill proposed a bridge connecting Vashon Island to the mainland, sparking years of passionate debate about the island's future identity.
timeline_entries.details: The bridge proposal divided the island community. Proponents argued it would boost economic development and eliminate ferry dependence. Opponents, led by Alex Anderson and the anti-bridge committee, warned it would destroy the island's rural character and lead to 'Mercerization' — the rapid suburbanization that had transformed nearby Mercer Island after bridge construction. At a pivotal 1959 legislative session, Lt. Governor John Cherberg's procedural ruling effectively killed the bill, preserving Vashon's ferry-dependent identity for generations to come.

timeline_entries.title: Post-War Population and Suburban Pressure
timeline_entries.description: Post-WWII suburban expansion pressured Vashon Island as returning veterans and young families sought affordable rural land within commuting distance of Seattle and Tacoma.
timeline_entries.details: The 1950s brought significant demographic change to Vashon Island. GI Bill benefits enabled veterans to purchase homes, and the new state ferry system made commuting feasible. The island's population grew from approximately 3,000 to 4,500 during the decade. New subdivisions were platted, and the tension between growth and rural preservation became a defining theme of island politics that continues to the present day.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Heritage Museum Founded
timeline_entries.description: The Vashon-Maury Island Heritage Association was founded to preserve the island's history, later becoming the Vashon Heritage Museum.
timeline_entries.details: Concerned about the rapid loss of pioneer-era structures and oral histories, community members including Jean Findlay established the heritage association. The organization began collecting photographs, documents, and artifacts from island families. Over the decades it grew into the Vashon Heritage Museum, which now houses the most comprehensive collection of Vashon Island historical materials and serves as the primary resource for researchers studying the island's past.

timeline_entries.title: Ox-Team Skid Roads Built for Logging Operations
timeline_entries.description: Logging crews built ox-team skid roads across Vashon Island to drag felled timber from interior forests to shoreline loading points.
timeline_entries.details: The earliest logging on Vashon Island relied on teams of oxen pulling logs along 'skid roads' — paths of greased logs laid perpendicular to the route of travel. These primitive roads cut through dense old-growth forest, creating the first significant human-made pathways across the island's interior. The ecological impact was substantial: the roads cleared corridors through ancient forest, altered drainage patterns, and created the first large-scale disturbance of the island's forest canopy since the last glacial period.

timeline_entries.title: Port Gamble Mill's Vashon Timber Operations
timeline_entries.description: The Puget Mill Company at Port Gamble, owned by Maine lumber barons Pope and Talbot, systematically harvested Vashon Island's old-growth timber for the Pacific lumber trade.
timeline_entries.details: Andrew J. Pope and William C. Talbot's Port Gamble mill had been operating since 1853 when they filed their first Vashon Island land claim in 1864. Their operations represented the extension of east-coast industrial capitalism to the Pacific Northwest. Massive Douglas fir, western red cedar, and Sitka spruce — some over 500 years old — were felled and towed in log rafts to the Port Gamble mill for processing. The timber was shipped to San Francisco, the Hawaiian Islands, and markets throughout the Pacific. By the 1890s, much of the island's accessible old-growth forest had been cut.

timeline_entries.title: Donation Land Claim Act Opens Vashon to Settlement
timeline_entries.description: The Donation Land Claim Act of 1850, authored by Oregon Territory delegate Samuel Royal Thurston, provided the legal framework for claiming Vashon Island land — while explicitly excluding Black and Hawaiian settlers.
timeline_entries.details: The act granted up to 320 acres to single white male settlers and 640 acres to married couples who could demonstrate residence and cultivation of the land. It was a cornerstone of Manifest Destiny policy, designed to encourage American settlement of the Oregon Territory (which then included present-day Washington). Its racial exclusions reflected the era's systemic discrimination. On Vashon Island, the first claims under this act would not be filed until the 1860s, after logging operations had begun to open the dense forest.

timeline_entries.title: Hudson's Bay Company Influence Wanes on Puget Sound
timeline_entries.description: The Oregon Treaty of 1846 established the US-Canada border at the 49th parallel, ending British claims to Puget Sound and gradually diminishing the Hudson's Bay Company's commercial influence around Vashon Island.
timeline_entries.details: The HBC's Fort Nisqually had been the dominant European presence near Vashon Island since 1833, operating the Puget Sound Agricultural Company with extensive livestock and farming operations. After the Oregon Treaty, American settlers increasingly challenged the HBC's land claims. William Tolmie, the fort's Chief Factor, struggled to maintain British commercial interests as American territorial governance took hold. The transition from HBC fur trade economy to American settler economy fundamentally changed the dynamics of land use and indigenous relations in the waters around Vashon.

timeline_entries.title: Backbone Campaign Founded on Vashon Island
timeline_entries.description: Bill Moyer founded the Backbone Campaign on Vashon Island, pioneering 'artful activism' that combined creative arts with environmental and social justice advocacy.
timeline_entries.details: The Backbone Campaign became nationally recognized for its innovative protest tactics, including giant puppets, mobile stages, and creative direct action. Based on Vashon Island, it organized annual Action Camps that drew activists from across the country. Key campaigns included opposition to Lower Snake River dams (for salmon and orca protection), support for Standing Rock water protectors, and the ShellNO kayaktivist actions against Arctic drilling. The organization reflected Vashon's identity as a progressive, environmentally conscious community.

timeline_entries.title: Vashon Island Organic Farming Renaissance
timeline_entries.description: The back-to-the-land movement brought a new generation of organic farmers to Vashon Island, transforming the island into a Pacific Northwest center for sustainable agriculture.
timeline_entries.details: Beginning in the mid-1970s, young farmers drawn by Vashon's rural character and relatively affordable land began establishing organic farms on the island. Pioneers like Henning Sehmsdorf and Elizabeth Simpson founded S&S Homestead Farm as a model biodynamic operation. The Vashon Island Growers Association and the weekly Farmers Market became community institutions. By the 2000s, Vashon had one of the highest concentrations of organic farms per capita in Washington state, and organic agriculture had become central to the island's cultural identity and economic life.

timeline_entries.title: Bruce Haulman Begins Documenting Vashon History
timeline_entries.description: Historian Bruce Haulman began his decades-long project of comprehensively documenting Vashon Island history, creating vashonhistory.com and authoring multiple books on the island's past.
timeline_entries.details: Building on the work of earlier historians like Oliver Van Olinda and Marjorie Rose Stanley, Haulman brought academic rigor and digital accessibility to Vashon Island history. His website vashonhistory.com became the most comprehensive online resource for island history, while his regular columns in the Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber brought historical awareness to the wider community. His work ensured that the stories of indigenous peoples, pioneers, Japanese American farmers, and modern islanders would be preserved and accessible for future generations.

timeline_entries.title: Japanese American Farms Lost During Internment
timeline_entries.description: During the forced internment of Japanese Americans, Vashon Island's Japanese farming families lost their lands, crops, equipment, and livelihoods — devastating losses from which the community never fully recovered.
timeline_entries.details: When Executive Order 9066 forced the removal of all Japanese Americans from the West Coast, Vashon Island's Japanese farming families — including the Mukais, Matsudas, Sakais, and Hoshis — were given only days to dispose of property accumulated over decades. Most farms were sold at fire-sale prices or simply abandoned. Equipment, livestock, and stored crops were lost. The island's strawberry industry, which Japanese American farmers had built into a nationally significant operation, collapsed. After the war, only a handful of families returned to Vashon, and the community's agricultural legacy was largely erased from the landscape.

timeline_entries.title: Lucy Gerand Documents S'Homamish Place Names and Lifeways
timeline_entries.description: Puyallup elder Lucy Gerand provided anthropologist T.T. Waterman with detailed accounts of traditional sx̌ʷəbabš place names, village locations, and seasonal gathering patterns on Vashon and Maury Islands.
timeline_entries.details: Lucy Gerand's interviews with Waterman in the 1920s preserved knowledge of indigenous place names and resource gathering sites that would otherwise have been lost. She described the seasonal round — spring fish camps, summer berry gathering, fall salmon runs, and winter village life — that had sustained the S'Homamish people for millennia. Her testimony documented at least five major village sites on Vashon and Maury Islands, including sites at Quartermaster Harbor, Burton, and the island's western shore. These accounts remain among the most important primary sources for understanding the island's pre-contact indigenous geography.

timeline_entries.title: Betty MacDonald Writes 'Onions in the Stew' on Vashon
timeline_entries.description: Author Betty MacDonald published 'Onions in the Stew,' a humorous memoir of island life on Vashon that introduced the island to a national audience.
timeline_entries.details: Betty MacDonald (born Anne Elizabeth Campbell Bard, 1907) moved to Vashon Island on April 24, 1942, after marrying Donald C. MacDonald. She had already achieved fame with 'The Egg and I' (1945), which was serialized in The Atlantic before publication and became a bestseller inspiring the Ma and Pa Kettle film series. 'Onions in the Stew' (1955) was a direct memoir of her Vashon years — a humorous account of ferry dependency, eccentric neighbors, gardening misadventures, and raising teenage daughters on the island. She also wrote the beloved Mrs. Piggle-Wiggle children's series while living on Vashon. U.S. Senator Richard Neuberger compared her humor to Mark Twain. Her Vashon home was approximately a quarter-mile south of Dolphin Point on the east side of the island. She died of cancer in Seattle on February 7, 1958, age 50.

timeline_entries.title: First Vashon Island Strawberry Festival
timeline_entries.description: The Vashon Island Commercial Club organized the first Strawberry Festival, celebrating the island's booming berry industry that was shipping over 120,000 crates of strawberries annually.
timeline_entries.details: The Strawberry Festival was organized in 1909 by the Vashon Island Commercial Club to promote the island's signature crop. That year, Vashon was shipping more than 120,000 crates of strawberries annually. The Burton Fair advertised 'Eat 20 miles of strawberries.' The festival became the island's premier community event. During WWII it was suspended, then briefly rebranded as the Peach Festival (1946-1948), Vashon Festival (1949), Harvest Festival (1951), and Island Festival (1952-1983). Renamed the Strawberry Festival in 1984, it now draws tens of thousands of visitors annually and remains the island's largest event. Community members have re-established small test plots of the heritage Marshall variety.

timeline_entries.title: John Martinolich Founds Shipbuilding Company at Dockton
timeline_entries.description: Croatian-born shipbuilder John A. Martinolich founded his own shipyard at Dockton, launching a career that would make him the 'King of Purse Seiners' and establish Dockton as a major Pacific Coast shipbuilding center.
timeline_entries.details: John A. Martinolich was born on the island of Mali Lussin, Croatia, and began working in his father's shipyard at age 10. He emigrated in 1896 and settled in Dockton, finding work as a shipwright at the existing dry dock. In 1904, he left the main yard and founded the John A. Martinolich Shipbuilding Company. His first vessel was the steamer Vashon, completed in 1905. Over the following decades he built dozens of vessels: Verona (1910), Nisqually (1911), Calista (1911), Florence J. (1914), F.G. Reeves (1916), Vashona (1921), and the ferry Whidby (1923). By the 1920s, he was known as the 'King of Purse Seiners' for developing the West Coast purse seiner — a deep-draft fishing boat design that became the standard for the Pacific fishing fleet.
